claims: The natural numbers are the nonnegative whole numbers, represented on the number line as points obtained by starting at 0 and moving right by a whole unit length any number of times.

The Peano axioms establish that every element of the set can be obtained by starting from 0 and applying the successor operation ('plus one') some finite number of times; consequently, every natural number is either 0 or the successor of a unique natural number.

The rules describing the natural numbers are ( | 0 ) and ( n | n + 1 ), where the first rule means '0 is a natural number' and the second means 'if n is a natural number, then n + 1 is a natural number'.
A set-theoretic construction of the natural numbers, known as von Neumann natural numbers, encodes them as sets.
In this construction, the natural number 0 is identified with the empty set ∅ (0 vN = ∅), and the successor operation s is defined by s(n vN) = n + vN for all n vN in the set.
The set, the zero element, and the successor function together define a notion of natural numbers.

While the book adopts the convention that natural numbers start at 0, this is a matter of taste or convenience rather than a provable fact; some authors define them as positive whole numbers starting at 1.
The natural numbers are closed under addition and multiplication, meaning that whenever a and b are natural numbers, a + b and ab are also natural numbers.
However, they are not closed under subtraction or division, as demonstrated by the fact that 1 and 2 are natural numbers, but 1 - 2 and 1/2 are not.

The recursion theorem for the natural numbers allows defining a function h: N → X by specifying h(0) and h(n + 1) in terms of h(n), which is possible because every natural number is obtained from 0 by adding one a finite number of times.
The integers are the whole numbers, represented on the number line by points obtained by starting at 0 and moving in either direction by the unit length any number of times.
This construction gives rise to the integers, which can be used for measuring the difference between two natural numbers.
The set of all integers is denoted by Z.
Every integer has a finite description as a finite string of digits, possibly modified by a minus sign, such as 7 or −15213, and the set Z is countable.
The integers are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication, meaning that whenever a and b are integers, so are a + b, a - b, and ab.
Although addition, subtraction, and multiplication of two integers yield another integer, the same is not true of division; this behavior of division is what makes the integers interesting.
Every integer is a rational number, as a rational number is defined as a real number expressible as a fraction whose numerator is an integer and whose denominator is a nonzero integer.
A rational number is a real number that can be expressed as a fraction whose numerator is an integer and whose denominator is a nonzero integer.
a real number x is a rational number if and only if there exist integers a and b, with b ≠ 0, such that x = a/b
The set of all rational numbers is denoted by Q
Rational numbers are constructed from the integers by formalising the concept of the 'ratio' of two integers
Every integer is a rational number
the square of every rational number is a rational number
The set Q is a field
rational numbers can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided (provided the divisor is nonzero)
if x and y are rational numbers, then x + y, x - y, and xy are also rational numbers
if y ≠ 0, then x/y is a rational number
The set Q is countable
Between any two distinct rational numbers, there is a third distinct rational number
A positive rational number q can be expressed as the ratio of two nonzero natural numbers a and b such that the only natural number dividing both a and b is 1
Rational numbers are central to several areas of mathematics, including algebraic number theory and algebraic geometry
Real numbers are defined as the numbers represented by points on the real number line, which consists of an infinite line with a fixed zero point and a fixed unit length.
In a more abstract construction, real numbers can be identified with particular subsets of the rational numbers, specifically the set of rational numbers less than a given real number.
The set of real numbers, equipped with addition, multiplication, and the ordering relation, forms a complete ordered field; any two complete ordered fields are essentially the same.
They are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (provided the denominator is not zero).
Addition and multiplication are both commutative and associative.
Addition and subtraction are inverse operations, as are multiplication and division (for non-zero divisors).
(a + b) - b = a
(a/b) * b = a
Real numbers include rational numbers, which are defined as real numbers expressible as a fraction of two integers with a non-zero denominator.

The existence of square roots for non-negative real numbers is also a property of this set, where the square root of a non-negative real number a is defined as the positive real number whose square is a.
The set of real numbers is also used to define sequences, where a sequence is a function from the natural numbers to the real numbers.
An irrational number is defined as a real number that is not rational.
there is no standard single letter used to express the set of irrational numbers; instead, the set is written as the set difference of the real numbers and the rational numbers (R
The number √2 is a specific real number that is irrational.
Proving that a real number is irrational is not particularly easy in general.
if r is a rational number and a is an irrational number, then r + a is irrational.
there exist irrational numbers a and b such that their product ab is rational.
The irrationality of √2 also implies that √2 cannot be an integer.

the failure of completeness is an intrinsic property of the rational numbers, and proofs of this failure can be constructed without using irrational numbers, although doing so makes the proof significantly longer.
A complex number is an expression of the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers.
The set of all complex numbers is denoted by C.
This number system is constructed by extending the real numbers (R) by adjoining a square root of −1.
while quadratic polynomials with a negative discriminant have no real roots, the set of complex numbers contains roots for all quadratic polynomials and, in fact, all non-constant polynomials.
Arithmetic operations with complex numbers are performed by treating the imaginary unit i as a variable and simplifying powers of i using the fact that i² = −1.
i² = −1
Division by a complex number is a more complicated operation that requires the real components a and b to not both be zero.
a complex number α is defined as algebraic if p(α) = 0 for some nonzero polynomial p(x) over the rational numbers (Q).
Divisibility is a relation on the set of integers, denoted by the expression 'x divides y'.
A defining characteristic of this concept is that it is formulated in terms of multiplication rather than the arithmetic operation of division.
stating that 0 divides 0 simply means that 0 can be multiplied by an integer to obtain 0
if a divides b, then b can be expressed as the product of a and some integer k

This relation is foundational to number theory, as it allows for the generalization of concepts like the greatest common divisor to settings where a natural notion of order, such as the number line, is not available.
the divisibility relation partially orders the set of natural numbers
it does not partially order the set of integers because it lacks antisymmetry on Z
A set is defined as a collection of objects, and the objects contained within the set are called elements of the set.
When X is a set and x is an object, the notation x ∈ X is used to indicate that x is an element of X.

Sets are fundamental mathematical objects that serve as the basis for interpreting real-world situations mathematically; for example, in probability, the outcomes of a die roll are interpreted as the elements of the set {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, and an event is interpreted as a subset of that set.

Sets can be specified by listing their elements, such as A = {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, or by describing properties that their elements must satisfy, such as the set of all sets that are not elements of themselves.

The concept of elements is central to defining more complex structures, including the union of a collection of sets (the set of all objects that are elements of at least one of the sets) and the intersection of a collection of sets (the set of all objects that are elements of all of the sets).

Sets can also contain other sets as elements, and the relationship between elements and sets is used to define concepts like equivalence classes, where the equivalence class of an element a in a set X is the set of elements of X that a is equivalent to.
Set-builder notation is a means of specifying a set in terms of the properties its elements satisfy.
It is particularly useful for defining sets based on the properties they satisfy, and is often more concise than list notation, which may be unsuitable when the set cannot be clearly listed.
The notation is written as { x | p(x) }, where p(x) is a statement involving a variable x.
This expression denotes the set of all mathematical objects x making the statement p(x) true.
An object a is an element of the set { x | p(x) } if and only if the property p(x) is true when a is substituted for x in the expression p(x); that is, a ∈ { x | p(x) } if and only if p(a) is true.
The comprehension axiom implies that anything that can be defined using set-builder notation { x | p(x) } is a set.
However, in some contexts, not all expressions of the form { x | p(x) } define sets, as some approaches restrict how set-builder notation can be used to avoid paradoxes.
For example, the set { x | x = x } equals the universal set U, which is not an element of U.
Set-builder notation is also used to describe indexed families of sets, such as { Ai | i ∈ I }, where Ai is a set specified for each i in the index set I.
Mathematical Proof (Introduction) is an introductory unit within the Proof Basics topic that prepares learners for the more rigorous treatment of mathematical proof in the rest of the textbook.
The unit previews concepts that will be introduced more formally later and includes starter proofs written without worrying too much about technicalities.

It addresses the structure and wording of the proof, and it introduces proof strategies such as proof by contradiction, which arises from the introduction rule for negation and is described as extremely useful.

a derivation of q from p is sufficient to establish the truth of p ⇒ q by the introduction rule for implication, and conversely, if p ⇒ q is a tautology, then q can be derived from p using the elimination rule for implication together with the assumption that p ⇒ q is true

The unit includes a template for a proof of ∀n ⩾ n0, p(n), where Step 1 is the base case, Step 2 is the induction step, the assumption p(n) in Step 2 is the induction hypothesis, and the goal p(n+1) in Step 2 is the induction goal.

The unit includes a proof involving a sequence of real numbers (xn) and real numbers a, b such that a < xn < b for each n ⩾ 0, where the existence of a and b is justified by the boundedness of the sequence.
The unit includes a proof when n = 2, which is a specific case of a more general proof.
A proposition is a statement to which it makes sense to assign a truth value, which can be either true or false, and cannot be both.

Propositions serve as the fundamental building blocks of logical structure; for instance, the statements 'c divides b', 'b divides a', and 'c divides a' are all propositions in their own right, even when they appear inside a more complex proposition.
The logical structure of such complex propositions can be examined by replacing these simpler propositions with symbols called propositional variables.
A statement involving a free variable, such as 'x is divisible by 7', is not a proposition in its own right.
However, it becomes a proposition as soon as a particular numerical value is substituted for the variable from its domain of discourse.
For example, if x refers to an integer, substituting 28 yields the true proposition '28 is divisible by 7', while substituting 41 yields the false proposition '41 is divisible by 7'.
Propositions can also involve quantified statements, such as the existential claim that a polynomial f(x) has a real root, which is expressed as ∃x ∈ R, f(x) = 0.
While propositions are essential, relying solely on them without the ability to handle variables and predicates would halt mathematical reasoning pretty quickly.
Logical connectives are operators used to form more complex expressions representing propositions by connecting together simpler ones.
The standard symbols for these connectives include ∧ (which represents 'and'), ∨ (which represents 'or'), and ¬ (which represents 'not').

In the context of set theory and probability, these logical operators correspond to specific set operations: 'or' is interpreted as union, 'and' as intersection, and 'not' as relative complement in the sample space.

The distinction between conjunction ('and') and disjunction ('or') is fundamental to logical structure, as seen in the application of de Morgan's laws where the negation of a union results in a conjunction of negations.

A truth table is a structured representation of a propositional formula that systematically evaluates its truth value under every possible assignment of truth values to its constituent propositional variables.

The table is defined by having one row for each possible assignment of truth values to the formula's variables and one column for each subformula, including the individual propositional variables and the formula itself.
The entries within the table are the truth values of these subformulae.
The construction of a truth table for a complex formula involves combining the truth tables of its individual logical operators.

For instance, when evaluating a formula with three variables, the truth values for intermediate subformulae are determined by looking at the relevant columns to the left and comparing them with the truth tables for the specific logical operators involved, such as conjunction.

This process allows for the streamlined evaluation of logical equivalences and the proof of logical properties, such as demonstrating that two formulas are logically equivalent by showing they have the same truth values for all assignments of their constituent variables.
a tautology is a proposition or logical formula that is true, no matter how truth values are assigned to its component propositional variables and predicates
This concept is the opposite of a contradiction
the term has a precise definition in this context, distinct from its colloquial usage
p ∨ (¬p), which is identified as the law of excluded middle
p ⇒ (q ⇒ p)
any tautology may be assumed in any proof of a proposition p
a derivation of q from p is sufficient to establish the truth of p ⇒ q by the introduction rule for implication (⇒I)
if q can be derived from p, then p ⇒ q is a tautology
if p ⇒ q is a tautology, then q can be derived from p using the elimination rule for implication (⇒E) together with the assumption that p ⇒ q is true
the concept of tautology also appears in the definition of the Lindenbaum-Tarski algebra for propositional logic over P
[s] ≡ ⊢ [t] ≡ if and only if s ⇒ t is a tautology
A contradiction is a proposition that is known or assumed to be false.
In symbolic logic, the symbol ⊥ is used to represent a contradiction.
Examples of contradictions include the assertion that 0 = 1, that √2 is rational, or that the equation x² = -1 has a solution x ∈ R.
A tautology is the opposite of a contradiction.
In proofs, a contradiction is often derived to show that an assumption is false.
if an assumption in a proof has the form ¬p, then any derivation of p leads to a contradiction.
If a contradiction is assumed, any consequence may be derived.

A common application of proof by contradiction is when proving a statement of the form ∀n ⩾ n0, p(n) (for some n0 ∈ N) by contradiction: if it is false, then there is a counterexample to p(n), and so the set of all counterexamples is inhabited—we prove that the set of all counterexamples has infinite descent, leading to the desired contradiction.
Another example is proving that if x is irrational then -x and 1/x are irrational by contradiction.
In both cases, we arrive at a contradiction, which allows us to conclude that the original assumption was false.

A predicate is defined as a symbol p together with a specified list of free variables x1, x2, ..., xn (where n is a natural number) and, for each free variable xi, a specification of a set Xi called the domain of discourse (or range) of xi.
The standard notation for a predicate is p(x1, x2, ..., xn), which is used to make the variables explicit.
The statements represented by predicates are those that become propositions when specific values are substituted for their free variables from their respective domains of discourse.

the statement 'x is divisible by 7' can be represented by a predicate p(x) whose only free variable x has the set of integers Z as its domain of discourse; substituting 28 yields the true proposition '28 is divisible by 7', while substituting 41 yields the false proposition '41 is divisible by 7'
the expression '2n - 1 is prime' is represented by a predicate p(n) with one free variable n whose domain of discourse is the set N of natural numbers
A predicate with no free variables is precisely a propositional variable, meaning that the notion of a predicate generalizes that of a propositional variable

Predicates can also involve multiple variables, such as the expression 'x - y is rational', which is represented by a predicate q(x, y) with free variables x and y whose domain of discourse is the set R of real numbers

Predicates are also used in contexts involving sets, such as letting X be a set and p(x) be a predicate, or letting X and Y be sets and p(x, y) be a predicate with free variables x in X and y in Y, or letting E be an empty set and p(x) be a predicate with one free variable x with domain of discourse E
The universal quantifier is the logical operator denoted by the symbol ∀, which makes precise the meaning of the phrase 'for all'.
It is one of the two main quantifiers used throughout mathematics, the other being the existential quantifier.
Formally, if p(x) is a logical formula with a free variable x whose range is X, then the expression ∀x ∈ X, p(x) is a logical formula defined by specific rules.
The primary rule for this quantifier, labeled (∀I), states that if p(x) can be derived from the assumption that x is an arbitrary element of X, then ∀x ∈ X, p(x) holds.
This quantifier is used to assert that a property is true for every element in a specified domain, distinguishing it from quantifiers that assert the existence of at least one element.
The existential quantifier is a fundamental logical operator used in mathematics to assert that at least one object in a specified domain satisfies a given property.
It is represented by the symbol ∃ and is one of the two main quantifiers used throughout mathematics, the other being the universal quantifier.
The expression '∃ x ∈ X, p(x)' denotes the statement that there exists an element x in the set X such that the property p(x) is true.
This quantifier is distinct from the unique existential quantifier, which is represented by the symbol ∃! and asserts that there is exactly one such element.
The existential quantifier is used to formalize statements such as 'a polynomial f(x) has a real root,' which is expressed as ∃ x ∈ R, f(x) = 0.

Proving existentially quantified statements involves demonstrating the existence of at least one element that satisfies the condition, a process that is distinct from proving universal statements or assuming such statements in logical arguments.
In the context of logical formulae, which are expressions built from predicates using logical operators and quantifiers, variables are classified as either free or bound.
A variable is considered free if it makes sense to substitute particular elements of its domain of discourse into the statement; otherwise, the variable is bound.
Expressions that refer to how many elements of a set make a statement true, such as 'there exists' and 'every', turn free variables into bound variables.
The truth value of a logical formula depends on its free variables according to the rules for logical operators and quantifiers.
in the expression 'there exist integers a and b such that x = a2 + b2', x is a free variable while a and b are bound variables.
in the expression 'every even natural number n ⩾ 2 is divisible by k', k is a free variable and n is a bound variable.
These classifications are essential for understanding how logical formulae function and how their truth values are determined.
Logical equivalence is a relation on the set of all logical formulae, specifically an equivalence relation on the set of propositional formulae.
Two propositional formulae are logically equivalent if and only if their truth values are the same under any assignment of truth values to their constituent propositional variables.

This notion captures the sense in which two formulae 'mean the same thing' and allows for the transformation of a logical formula into a different but equivalent form, which helps identify a wider range of feasible proof strategies.
logical equivalence is defined in terms of derivation in each direction, and that the biconditional symbol is the conjunction of two implications.
Truth tables are used to prove logical equivalence by checking that the formulae have identical columns.
∀x∈X, ∀y∈Y, p(x,y) and ∀y∈Y, ∀x∈X, p(x,y) are logically equivalent
p⇒q and (¬q)⇒(¬p) are logically equivalent
The law of double negation is a logical equivalence used in indirect proof techniques.
De Morgan's laws are a family of logical equivalences that exhibit a duality between conjunction (∧) and disjunction (∨), and between universal (∀) and existential (∃) quantifiers.
The laws are used to negate complex logical statements by distributing the negation across the operators and swapping the paired operators.
The source establishes that these laws hold for logical operators, quantifiers, and set operations (union and intersection), and are generalized to Boolean algebras.

negating an existentially quantified statement (¬∃) is equivalent to a universally quantified negation (∀¬), and negating a universally quantified statement (¬∀) is equivalent to an existentially quantified negation (∃¬)
The source notes that these laws are frequently used in proofs and that the distinction between logical equivalence (≡) and material implication (⇒) is relevant to their application.

The contrapositive of a proposition of the form p ⇒ q is the proposition ¬ q ⇒ ¬ p.
Every implication is logically equivalent to its contrapositive.
This logical equivalence allows for proofs by contraposition, a method where a statement is proven by establishing the truth of its contrapositive.
The converse of a conditional is a logical relationship where one implication is the converse of another.
In the context of solving equations, proving the converse is necessary to ensure the validity of the solution process.
This unit is distinct from the concept of an inverse function, which involves finding a function that reverses the mapping of another function.
A subset of a set X is a set U such that U is contained in X.
The subset relation, denoted by ⊆, is a relation on the power set P(X) for any set X.
every set is a subset of itself, meaning X ⊆ X for all sets X
To prove that a set U is a subset of a set X, it suffices to take an arbitrary element a ∈ U and prove that a ∈ X.
A k-element subset of X is a subset U ⊆ X such that |U| = k
the number of ways of selecting a k-element subset of [n] and an ℓ-element subset of [k] is given by the product of the binomial coefficients (n choose k) and (k choose ℓ)
This is equivalent to the number of ways of selecting a k-element subset of [n] and then an ℓ-element subset of the k-element subset that was just selected
every subset G ⊆ X × Y is the graph of a unique relation R from X to Y
every finite set is a proper subset of another finite set
every inhabited subset of the set of nonnegative rational numbers has a least element
The power set of a set X, denoted P(X), is a set whose elements are the subsets of X.
The existence of P(X) for all sets X is asserted by the power set axiom, which functions as a construction rule for creating new sets from sets already known to exist.
The power set P(X) is partially ordered by the subset relation (⊆).
Within this structure, the relation satisfies reflexivity, meaning that for any U in P(X), U is a subset of U.
It also satisfies antisymmetry, meaning that if U and V are in P(X) and U is a subset of V and V is a subset of U, then U equals V.
For any set X, the power set lattice (P(X), ⊆) is distributive.
The power set of the natural numbers is an uncountable set.
Some authors use the notation 2^X to refer to the power set of a set X.
Power sets are often a point of confusion because they bring the property of being a subset of one set to that of being an element of another.
The empty set, also known as the null set, is defined as the set with no elements.
It is denoted by the symbol ∅, and some authors write {} instead, since {} is simply the empty set expressed in list notation.
The existence of the empty set is asserted by the empty set axiom, which states that there is a set with no elements.
While the axiom asserts existence, the empty set axiom is in fact redundant in the presence of the other axioms.

The uniqueness of the empty set is established by the axiom of extensionality, which implies that any two empty sets must be equal since they both contain the same elements—namely, no elements at all.
This uniqueness allows us to talk about 'the' empty set.
To prove that a set X is empty, one assumes that X is inhabited—that is, that there is some element a ∈ X—and derives a contradiction.
The empty set is finite, and it serves as the graph of a relation on N.
In the context of relations, the empty relation from a set X to a set Y is the relation ∅ X, Y.
The empty set also appears in the context of pairwise disjoint sets, where a collection of sets is pairwise disjoint if for all A, B in the collection, if A ≠ B, then A ∩ B is empty.
The empty set is a fundamental example of a set, and its properties are central to the study of sets.
Set equality is defined by the principle that two sets are equal if and only if they contain exactly the same elements.
This extensional notion of equality is formalized in ZF set theory by the axiom of extensionality, which states that if two sets have the same elements, then they are equal.
the sets {1, 2, 3}, {3, 2, 1}, and {1, 2, 3, 3, 3} are all equal because they possess the identical elements, regardless of the order in which they are listed or the presence of duplicate entries.
the equality relation (=) on any set X is a specific relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
It is reflexive because a = a for all a in X; symmetric because if a = b, then b = a; and transitive because if a = b and b = c, then a = c.
Consequently, the equality relation is an equivalence relation on X.
Furthermore, the equality relation is antisymmetric, meaning that if a = b and b = a, then a = b.
The equality relation is unique in this regard: it is the only relation on a set X that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and antisymmetric.
To prove that two sets A and B are equal, a standard strategy is to prove that A is a subset of B and that B is a subset of A (double containment).
This follows from the definition of set equality, which implies that if U and V are subsets of a set X such that U is a subset of V and V is a subset of U, then U = V.

Another method for proving set equality involves showing that the characteristic functions of the sets are equal; specifically, to prove that two subsets A and B of a set X are equal, it suffices to prove that their characteristic functions are identical.
The union of a collection of sets is defined as the set of all objects that are elements of at least one of the sets in the collection.
This operation allows for the discussion of the set of objects that appear in at least one of the sets in a collection.
The union of any family of sets exists and is a set.
Formally, if F = { Xi | i ∈ I } is a family of sets, the set U = ⋃ i ∈ I Xi exists.
The union of A0, A1, ..., An−1 is denoted by the union symbol.
In the context of probability, the events { X = e } for e ∈ E are mutually exclusive, and their union is the sample space.
The union of A and B is distinct from the disjoint union of A and B, which is denoted A ⊔ B and involves the sets A × { 0 } and B × { 1 }.
There are many algebraic results concerning what happens when different set operations, such as intersection and union, are combined.
The intersection of a collection of sets is the set of all objects that are elements of all of the sets in the collection.
For a collection of just two sets, the intersection is written as A ∩ B.
the set [0, ∞) ∩ Q is the intersection of [0, ∞) and Q, which is the set of all objects that are elements of both [0, ∞) and Q.
Since the elements of [0, ∞) are the non-negative real numbers and the elements of Q are the rational numbers, [0, ∞) ∩ Q is the set of all non-negative rational numbers.
if I is inhabited, the intersection of the sets Xi for i ∈ I is denoted by XI.
A careful examination of the definition reveals that X∅ = X.
The intersection operation is one of the various operations that can be performed on sets, alongside union and others.
In topology, the intersection of finitely many open sets is open, but the intersection of infinitely many open sets might not be open.

The complement of a set A is defined as the set of all objects that are not elements of A, typically denoted by Ac or A.
the complement of a set is not generally a set within the universe of discourse
the complement of the empty set is the entire union of discourse
A c = Ω // A for a sample space Ω or A c = X // A for a fixed set X

A lattice is complemented if every element x ∈ X has a complement
a Boolean algebra is a complemented distributive lattice with a greatest element and a least element
The complement of an event A ⊆ Ω is the event Ω // A ⊆ Ω
The cartesian product is a set operation used to construct sets of ordered lists, where the sets in the product determine what kind of object the corresponding term in the list can be.

Intuitively, by devising a step-by-step procedure for specifying an element of a set X, one is constructing a cartesian product of the form ∏_{k=1}^n X_k, where X_k is the set of choices to be made in the k-th step.
The notation for the cartesian product includes the symbols ×, ∏, and A_k.
A specific notation, A_k, is used to denote the k-fold cartesian product.
The cardinal product of cardinal numbers κ and λ is the cardinal number κ · λ, which is defined as the cardinality of the cartesian product.
Similarly, the indexed cardinal product is the cardinality of the indexed cartesian product.
Let {X_i | i ∈ I} be a family of sets indexed by a set I; the indexed cartesian product of the sets X_i for i ∈ I is a defined concept.

Elements of cartesian products do not depend on one another, and so the set of sequences of choices made cannot necessarily be expressed as a cartesian product of two sets if the possible choices available in one step depend on the choice made in a previous step.
The axiom of choice states that the cartesian product of every family of inhabited sets is inhabited.
An indexed family of sets over a set I is a specification of a set Ai for each element i in I.
This collection is described in set-builder notation as { Ai | i ∈ I }.
The set I is called the indexing set, and the elements of I are called indices; specifically, an element i ∈ I serves as the index of the corresponding set Ai in the family.
The notation { [0, 1 + 1/n) | n ≥ 1 } expresses the collection of sets of the form [0, 1 + 1/n) as an indexed family of sets.

Indexed families of sets serve as the foundational structure for defining indexed operations, such as the indexed disjoint union, the indexed cartesian product, and the indexed cardinal sum of a family of sets or cardinal numbers.
The domain is defined as the set of all possible inputs for a function or relation.
In the context of a function M, the domain is the set I of all possible inputs, while the codomain is the set O containing all possible outputs.
Similarly, for a relation R, the set X is designated as the domain of R.
The domain is also used in the definition of predicates, where for each free variable, a specified set is called the domain of discourse or range.
It is important to specify the domain when defining a function, as it determines the set of elements for which the function is defined.
A function with an empty domain has no values, and every function with an empty codomain has an empty domain.
The domain is a fundamental component in the definition of functions and relations, and it is used to specify the set of inputs for which a function or relation is defined.
The codomain, also referred to as the target, is the set Y associated with a function f, where the set X is the domain (or source).
In a functional mapping, the codomain is a set O containing all the possible 'outputs', while the function M is a rule specifying how an input is associated with the corresponding output.

A defining characteristic of the codomain is that it is not required to be fully utilized; it does not matter if some elements of the codomain are unaccounted for, as long as each element of the domain is associated with exactly one element of the codomain.
The codomain is a critical component in the specification of a function, as illustrated by the function r: (0,∞) → (0,∞), which is well-defined by the equation r(x)² = x for all x ∈ (0,∞).
r(x)² = x for all x ∈ (0,∞)
This example highlights the importance of specifying both the domain and codomain when defining a function.
In the context of relations, two relations R and S are equal if and only if they have the same domain X and codomain Y, and for all x ∈ X and y ∈ Y, x R y if and only if x S y.
The codomain also plays a role in the specification of the empty function, which is the unique function ∅ → X with codomain X.
The codomain is distinct from the domain, which is the set of all possible inputs, and from the image of a function, which is the set of actual outputs.
The codomain is a fundamental concept in the study of functions and relations, and its proper specification is essential for the rigorous definition and comparison of mathematical objects.
The image of a function is a subset of its domain.
The image of any set under any function is a set.
Let f: X → Y be a function and let U ⊆ X. The image of U under f is the subset f [ U ] ⊆ Y
Function composition is the operation on functions that involves applying a sequence of functions one-by-one until a desired result is reached.
It is considered the most important operation on functions, analogous to how union and intersection are operations on sets.
In the notation g ◦ f, the function applied first is written last; this ordering is consistent with the convention that the argument to a function is written after the function.
The composition of two functions f and g is defined such that for all x in the domain, the composite function h is given by h(x) = g(f(x)).
Composition of functions is associative, meaning that for composable functions f, g, and h, the equality h ◦ (g ◦ f) = (h ◦ g) ◦ f holds.
if F is a function from X to Y and G is a function from Y to Z, and both F and G are injective, then their composition G ◦ F is also injective.
if G(F(A)) = G(F(B)), the injectivity of G implies F(A) = F(B), and the injectivity of F implies A = B.
The identity function is a class of functions that are described as very simple yet important enough to warrant a formal definition.
The identity function on a set X is denoted as id X.
there is a handy lemma that provides a convenient means of proving when a function is the identity function.
x + 0 = x for all x in X
x · 1 = x for all x in X
The identity function is also referenced in the context of the set [n], denoted as id [n].
An inverse function for a function f: X → Y is a function g: Y → X that acts as both a left inverse and a right inverse for f.
A left inverse (or post-inverse) for f is a function g: Y → X such that g ◦ f = idX.
A right inverse (or pre-inverse) for f is a function g: Y → X such that f ◦ g = idY.
A two-sided inverse is a function g: Y → X which is both a left inverse and a right inverse for f.
If a function has both a left and a right inverse, they must be equal; consequently, every bijective function has a unique inverse.
An involution is a function that is its own inverse.

When proving a function f: X → Y is bijective by finding an inverse g: Y → X, it is important to check that g is both a left inverse and a right inverse for f; proving only that g is a left inverse establishes only that f is injective.
If f is injective and X is inhabited, then f has a left inverse.
If f has a right inverse, then f is surjective.
Addition and subtraction by a real number are inverse operations; likewise for multiplication and division.
(a+b)−b = a
(a/b)×b = a
A function f: X → Y is injective (or one-to-one) if, for all a, b ∈ X, if f(a) = f(b) then a = b.
An injective function is also called an injection.
This property means that f sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs.
If f is injective, there exists a function g: f[X] → X such that x = g(f(x)) for all x ∈ X;
in this context, f acts as an encoding function and g as the corresponding decoding function.
If f and g are injective, then their composition g ◦ f is injective.
For finite sets X and Y, if |X| ≤ |Y|, a function f: X → Y is injective.
A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.
A function f: X → Y is surjective (or onto) if, for every element y in Y, there exists an element x in X such that f(x) = y.
A surjective function is also called a surjection.
To prove that a function f: X → Y is surjective, it suffices to take an arbitrary element y ∈ Y and, in terms of y, find an element x ∈ X such that f(x) = y.
An alternative strategy for proving surjectivity is to find a right inverse: a function g: Y → X such that f(g(y)) = y for all y ∈ Y.
The condition that f is surjective is equivalent to the statement that Y = f[X], where f[X] denotes the image of X under f.
A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective; such a function is called a bijection.
In the context of function composition, if g ∘ f is bijective, then f is injective and g is surjective.
Surjectivity is also used to prove that a set is uncountable: it suffices to prove that no function f: N → X is surjective.

Examples of surjective functions include the remainder function r: Z → [n] (where [n] = {1, ..., n}) defined by r(a) being the remainder of a when divided by n, and the norm function f: R^n → R defined by f(x) = ||x||.
A function f: X → Y is bijective if it is both injective and surjective; such a function is also called a bijection.
To prove that a function is bijective, one can prove that it is injective and surjective.
Alternatively, a function can be proven bijective by finding an inverse g: Y → X; in this approach, it is important to check that g is both a left inverse and a right inverse for f.
If one only proves that g is a left inverse for f, then one has only proved that f is injective.
Every bijective function has a unique inverse, meaning that for any function f: X → Y, any two inverses for f are equal.
In the context of function composition, if g ◦ f is bijective, then f is injective and g is surjective.

The existence of a bijection between sets is also used to establish properties such as countability; for example, if a set is a composite of bijections, it is bijective, meaning the set is countably infinite.
Peano's axioms are a set of three properties, labeled (i), (ii), and (iii), that formalize the structure of the natural numbers.

The set of natural numbers is the canonical example of an inductively defined set, where every element can be obtained by starting from 0 and applying the successor operation ('plus one') some finite number of times.
every natural number is either 0 or is the successor of a unique natural number
The axioms serve as the foundation for deriving the weak and strong induction principles, which are powerful tools for proving results about natural numbers.
u + w = v + w implies u = v for all u, v, w in the natural numbers
can be proved by induction on w using only Peano's axioms without assuming the existence of a subtraction operation
The convention that natural numbers start at 0 is used in this context, though it is noted that other conventions are theoretically possible while still allowing the use of recursion and induction.
The well-ordering principle is a property of the natural numbers stating that if a set of natural numbers has at least one element, then it has a least element.

This property distinguishes the natural numbers from other number sets, such as the integers, which do not have a least element because for any integer a, a-1 is also an integer and is smaller than a.

The principle is equivalent to the assertion that no inhabited subset of the natural numbers has infinite descent; consequently, constructing an inhabited subset of the natural numbers with infinite descent yields a contradiction.
The well-ordering principle provides the underlying reason why induction and recursion can be performed on the natural numbers.

It is frequently used in proofs to establish the existence of a least element in a set of natural numbers, such as finding the least natural number a such that a rational number q can be expressed as a ratio of natural numbers, or finding the least element in a set of integers defined by a linear combination.
The principle also gives rise to a strategy for deriving contradictions by using a contradictory assumption to build a set of natural numbers with no least element.
The weak induction principle is a theorem concerning logical formulas with a free variable n in the natural numbers N.

The principle allows one to conclude that p(n) is true for all n greater than or equal to n0, provided two conditions are met: first, that p(n0) is true, and second, that for all n greater than or equal to n0, the implication p(n) implies p(n+1) holds.

The standard procedure for a proof by weak induction consists of two steps. Step 1 is the base case, where one proves p(n0). Step 2 is the induction step, where one fixes an arbitrary n such that n ⩾ n0, assumes p(n) (the induction hypothesis), and proves p(n+1).
Upon completing these steps, it follows by the weak induction principle that p(n) is true for all n ⩾ n0.
The weak induction principle is equivalent to the strong induction principle, despite the latter having a more powerful induction hypothesis.
The structural induction principle for the inductively defined set of natural numbers N is exactly the same as the weak induction principle.

The idea behind structural induction is the same as the idea behind weak induction: since every element a in a set A is of the form fσ(a) for some (possibly nullary) rule σ, if the truth of a property p is preserved by applying each constructor fσ, then p(x) must be true for all x in A.
In the case of nullary constructors, this amounts to checking that p(a) is true for each basic element a in A.
The base case is the initial verification step in a proof by induction, defined as the proof of the proposition p(n0) for the starting value n0.
In the standard template for proving ∀n ⩾ n0, p(n), the base case corresponds to 'Step 1', while the induction step corresponds to 'Step 2'.
The base case is distinct from the induction hypothesis (the assumption p(n) in the induction step) and the induction goal (the goal p(n+1) in the induction step).
In strong induction, the base case p(n0) serves as the starting point for the induction hypothesis, which encompasses p(k) for all n0 ⩽ k ⩽ n.

While a single base case is typical, proofs may require multiple base cases, such as p(n0), p(n0+1), ..., p(n1), particularly when proving results about recursively defined sequences where a general term depends on a fixed number of previous terms.
The base case is not strictly necessary to label explicitly from a mathematical perspective, but doing so helps the reader navigate the proof and identify the goal at each step.
Before proving the base case, it is helpful to write out exactly what is being proved in that part of the proof to clarify the aim.
The base case can be immediate or trivial in some contexts, such as when n=1 and the assertion reduces to a known property, or when the statement is self-evident for the initial element.
The base case may also involve verifying specific instances, such as proving p(4) is the statement 3·4 < 2^4, or verifying that a sequence term b0 = 1 = 2^0.
In some cases, the base case involves showing that a set is empty or that a function is a bijection for a single step.
The base case is a fundamental component of induction proofs, ensuring that the proposition holds for the initial value before the inductive step is applied.
A recursive definition is a method for defining expressions involving natural numbers by recursion, a process enabled by the recursion theorem.

This approach allows for the construction of mathematical objects such as addition, sequences, and other functions by specifying a base case and a rule that defines subsequent values based on previous ones.
addition can be defined recursively by stating that m + 0 = m and m + s(n) = s(m + n) for all n in the natural numbers
sequences can be defined recursively by providing initial values and a recurrence relation, such as a sequence defined by x0 = 0 and xn+1 = √2 + xn for all n ≥ 0
another sequence defined by a0 = 4, a1 = 9, and an = 5an−1 − 6an−2 for all n ≥ 2
Recursive definitions are also used to define logical quantifiers, such as the quantifier ∃=n, which means 'there are exactly n elements x in X such that p(x) is true.'
The recursive definition of a sequence can yield algorithms for computing mathematical expansions, such as base-b expansions.

recursive definitions can be used to prove properties of mathematical objects, such as proving that the recursive definition of the less-than-or-equal-to relation is equivalent to the definition of 'm ≤ n' as 'there exists k in N such that m + k = n.'
Strong induction is a proof principle for logical formulas with a free natural number variable.

It is structurally similar to weak induction, but its induction hypothesis is more powerful: in the induction step, the variable n is taken to be greater than or equal to a starting value n1, while the induction hypothesis assumes p(k) for all k such that n0 ≤ k ≤ n.
This allows the proof to assume the truth of the proposition for all previous values up to n, rather than just the immediately preceding value.
The principle is formally stated for cases with multiple base cases, where n0 < n1 are natural numbers, and the conclusion is that p(n) is true for all n ≥ n0.
Despite its name, strong induction is no stronger than weak induction; the two principles are equivalent.
Every proof by strong induction can be turned into a proof by weak induction by changing only the induction hypothesis, and vice versa.

In practice, proofs by strong induction often involve separating the base case from the induction step, and the quantification of variables in the induction step is crucial because it determines what may be assumed about the variables.
Proof by infinite descent is a proof strategy used to derive a contradiction from an assumption.
a set X of real numbers has infinite descent if, for every element x in X, there exists another element y in X such that y is strictly less than x
This property implies that an infinite, descending sequence of elements can be constructed from the set.
In the context of proof by contradiction, it suffices to use the assumption to prove the existence of an inhabited subset of the natural numbers that has infinite descent.
A common application involves proving a statement of the form that for all n greater than or equal to some n0, a property p(n) holds.
If the statement is false, the set of all counterexamples is inhabited; proving that this set has infinite descent leads to the desired contradiction.
the set of integers has infinite descent because for any integer n, n-1 is also an integer and is less than n
This strategy is distinct from strong induction, which is a method for proving universal statements directly rather than by contradiction.
A binary relation from a set X to a set Y is defined as a logical formula R(x, y) with two free variables, where x is an element of X and y is an element of Y.
This definition establishes the formal structure of a relation as a predicate over two domains.
The evidence provides specific instances of relations to illustrate this concept.
a relation ∼ on a set X can be defined for all x, y ∈ X by letting x ∼ y if and only if p(x) = p(y)
x ∼R y if and only if either x = y or the set {x, y} is equal to the set {a, b}
The equality relation = on any set X serves as a fundamental example of a relation.
It is reflexive because a = a for all a ∈ X.
It is also transitive because, for all a, b, c ∈ X, if a = b and b = c, then a = c
These examples demonstrate how relations are specified through logical conditions on their elements.
A relation R on a set X is reflexive if a R a for all a ∈ X.
a reflexive relation is one that relates every element of its domain to itself
R is reflexive if and only if ΔX ⊆ Gr(R)
a relation is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive
a relation is a partial order if it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive
the property depends on the set over which the relation is defined
the equality relation on any set X is reflexive because a = a for all a ∈ X
the relation defined on the real numbers by a R b if and only if b - a ∈ Q is reflexive because for all a ∈ R, a - a = 0 ∈ Q, so a R a
the relation 'x divides y' on the integers is also reflexive
the proper subset relation ⫋ is not reflexive
the subset relation ⊆ is reflexive on the power set P(X)
A relation R on a set X is symmetric if, for all a, b ∈ X, if a R b, then b R a.
This property implies that the direction of the relation does not matter: two elements are either each related to the other, or not related at all.
The equality relation on any set X is a symmetric relation, since for all a, b ∈ X, if a = b, then b = a.
Symmetry is an intrinsic property of the relation's graph; if two relations R and S have the same graph (Gr(R) = Gr(S)), then R is symmetric if and only if S is symmetric.
The number of symmetric relations on a set X with n elements is 2^(n(n-1)/2) · 2^n.
The evidence does not support the claim that every reflexive relation is symmetric, as this statement is factually incorrect in standard mathematics and contradicts the definition of symmetry.
A relation R on a set X is transitive if, for all a, b, c ∈ X, if a R b and b R c, then a R c.
Transitive relations are those for which we can skip over intermediate related elements; for example, we can deduce 0 < 3 from the facts that 0 < 1 and 1 < 2 and 2 < 3.
A fundamental property of transitive relations is that we can prove two elements a and b are related by finding a chain of related elements starting at a and finishing at b.
Let R be a relation on a set X. Then R is transitive if and only if, for any finite sequence x0, x1, ..., xn of elements of X such that xi−1 R xi for all i ∈ [n], we have x0 R xn.
Like symmetry, transitive is an intrinsic property of relations—that is, transitivity is not sensitive to the domain of the relation.
Given any set X, the equality relation = on X is transitive since, for all a, b, c ∈ X, if a = b and b = c, then a = c.

Transitivity is a component property used in the definitions of other relation types: a relation R on a set X is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; a relation R on a set X is a partial order if R is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; and a relation R on a set X is a strict partial order if it is irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive.
A relation R on a set X is antisymmetric if, for all a, b ∈ X, if a R b and b R a, then a = b.
The equality relation = on any set X is antisymmetric, since for all a, b ∈ X, if a = b and b = a, then a = b.
The order relation ⩽ on the real numbers R is antisymmetric, since for all a, b ∈ R, if a ⩽ b and b ⩽ a, then a = b.
The relation ⩽ on the set of cardinal numbers (Card) is also antisymmetric.
A relation R on a set X is a partial order if R is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
Antisymmetry is one of the three required properties for a relation to be a partial order.
A relation R is both symmetric and antisymmetric if and only if its graph Gr(R) is a subset of the diagonal subset ∆X of X × X.
The only reflexive, symmetric, and antisymmetric relation on a set X is the equality relation on X.
There is a unique relation on the natural numbers N that is reflexive, symmetric, and antisymmetric.
A relation R on a set X is a partial order if R is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
A set X together with a partial order R on X is called a partially ordered set, or poset for short, and is denoted (X, R).
The power set P(X) is partially ordered by the subset relation ⊆
any set X is partially ordered by its equality relation, a structure called the discrete order on X
Partial orders are in natural correspondence with strict partial orders, which are defined as relations that are irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.
x ≼ y if and only if x ≺ y or x = y, and x ≺ y if and only if x ≼ y and x ≠ y
every partial order can be strictified
the relation ⊢ is a partial order on a set A, meaning it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive
An equivalence relation on a set X is a relation on X that behaves like equality, providing a way to say that two elements of a set are 'similar' without having to be equal.
a relation R on a set X is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive
The equality relation = is an equivalence relation on any set X
a R b if and only if b - a is a rational number
(a, b) ∼ (c, d) if and only if ad = bc
The equivalence class of an element a in X is the set of elements of X that a is equivalent to
The quotient of a set by an equivalence relation is a partition of the set, and every partition of a set is the quotient by a unique equivalence relation
This establishes a bijection between equivalence relations on a set and partitions of that set
The quotient function for an equivalence relation ∼ on X sends each element of X to its ∼-equivalence class
An equivalence relation ∼ on a set X 'descends' to the equality relation = on the quotient X / ∼, allowing one to work with equality in the quotient rather than the equivalence relation itself
To prove that a relation is an equivalence relation, one must prove that it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive
An equivalence class is a set derived from a set X equipped with an equivalence relation ∼.
For an element a ∈ X, the ∼-equivalence class of a is the set of all elements of X that a is equivalent to.
This construction allows one to work with the equivalence classes of elements of X rather than the elements themselves, thereby treating two equivalent elements as being 'the same'.
The notation [a]∼ is used to denote the ∼-equivalence class of a.
The collection of all such classes forms the quotient set X/∼.
The quotient function for ∼ is the function q∼ that sends each element of X to its ∼-equivalence class.
The concept is used to make precise the idea that equivalence relations behave like equality, enabling the grouping of elements into distinct classes.
|X/∼|·k = n where k is the size of each class and n is the size of X

The equivalence class is distinct from the equivalence relation itself, which is the underlying relation on the set, and from the partition of a set, which is the collection of disjoint equivalence classes that cover the set.
A partition of a set X is a way of breaking X up into mutually disjoint subsets.
a partition of a set X is a set A ⊆ P(X) (that is, a set of subsets of X) such that the following conditions hold: (a) Every set A ∈ A is inhabited.
In the context of finite sets, a partition takes the form A = {Ai | i ∈ [n]} for some n ∈ N.
If X is a set and A = {Ai | i ∈ [n]} is a partition of X for some n ∈ N, such that each set Ai is finite, then X is finite, and |X| = ∑ i∈[n] |Ai|.
{E, O} is a partition of Z, with E ∩ O = ∅, implying the set has |E| + |O| elements.

Partitions are fundamentally linked to equivalence relations: the quotient of a set by an equivalence relation is a partition of the set, and every partition of a set is the quotient by a unique equivalence relation.
x ∼ y if and only if x and y are elements of the same set of the partition.
A set X is finite if the elements of X don’t go on forever.
a set X is finite if there exists a bijection f: [n] → X for some n ∈ N, where [n] denotes the set of natural numbers from 1 to n
If a set is not finite, it is called infinite.
The size of a finite set X is a natural number |X| ∈ N, which corresponds to the cardinality of the set when it is finite.
The union of a finite number of finite sets is finite.
Given two finite sets X and Y, their product X × Y is finite, and its size is given by |X × Y| = |X| · |Y|
This formula generalizes to products of any finite number of sets.
if X is a finite set and U ⊆ X, then the set difference X ∖ U is finite, and |X ∖ U| = |X| − |U|
The intersection of two finite sets is also finite.
If Y is a finite set of size n and there is an injection f: X → Y, then X is finite and |X| ≤ n
Partitions of finite sets consist of finitely many pieces, and if A = {Ai | i ∈ [n]} is a partition of a finite set X where each Ai is finite, then |X| = ∑ |Ai|
The concept of finiteness is foundational for comparing set sizes using injections, surjections, or bijections.
It also underpins the definition of countable sets, where the set of all finite subsets of a countable set is itself countable.
An infinite set is defined as a set that is not finite.
A set is considered finite if there exists a bijection between it and a finite set of natural numbers; consequently, a set is infinite if no such bijection exists for any natural number.
This definition is necessary because intuitive notions of size are insufficient for rigorous mathematical practice.
The set of natural numbers is infinite because it cannot be put into a one-to-one correspondence with any finite set.
The existence of infinite sets is also supported by the axiom of infinity, which asserts the existence of an infinite set using a set-theoretic construction called the successor set operation.
Infinite sets are distinct from countably infinite sets, which are a specific subclass of infinite sets that can be enumerated by a bijection with the natural numbers.
The cardinality of a finite set is a natural number that is equal to the size of the set.

While the size of a finite set X is a natural number |X| ∈ N, the cardinality of an arbitrary set is a cardinal number; however, if the set happens to be finite, this cardinal number is equal to the natural number given by its size.
Cardinality is understood as a measure of size that generalises the notion of size for finite sets to both finite and infinite sets.
Two finite sets X and Y have equal size if and only if there is a bijection X → Y
two sets X and Y have equal cardinality if and only if there is a bijection X → Y
The set of natural numbers N is a subset of the set of cardinal numbers Card
if X is finite, its cardinality |X| is equal to its size
A set is defined as countable if it is finite or countably infinite.
This concept is central to distinguishing between different sizes of infinity, specifically separating countable sets from uncountable ones.
A set X is countable if and only if it is at most as large as the set of natural numbers (N).

This equivalence allows for the proof of countability without explicitly constructing a bijection with N; instead, one can demonstrate that there exists a surjection from N onto X, or an injection from X into N.
More generally, a set X is countable if there exists an injection from X into any set C that is already known to be countable, or a surjection from such a set C onto X.
Countable sets possess several closure properties that facilitate their identification.
The union of countably many countable sets is countable.
The product of finitely many countable sets is countable, and the product of countably many countable sets is also countable.
Furthermore, if X is a countable set, the set of all finite subsets of X is countable.

This is established by noting that the set of all finite subsets of X is equal to the union over all k in N of the set of k-element subsets of X, which constitutes a union of countably many countable sets.
Intuitively, a set is countable if each of its elements has a finite description.
The set of natural numbers N is countable because every natural number can be expressed as a finite string of digits.
The set of integers Z is countable as every integer has a finite description as a finite string of digits, possibly modified by a minus sign.
The set of rational numbers Q is countable because every rational number has a finite description as a pair of integers.
The set of all finite subsets of N is also countable, as every finite subset of N has a finite expression in list notation.
These examples illustrate that countability is a property that can be extended to various mathematical structures, including sets of functions and random variables supported on countable sets.
A set X is countably infinite if there exists a bijection f from the set of natural numbers N to X.
This bijection f is called an enumeration of X.
A set X is countably infinite if and only if |X| = ℵ0, which is equivalent to saying that there is a bijection N → X, since ℵ0 = |N| = |X|.
A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite.

Proving that a set is countably infinite by finding an explicit bijection with the set of natural numbers can be overly burdensome, so closure properties of countable sets are developed to allow proving that a set is countable by relating it to sets that are already known to be countable.
A set X is countable if and only if X is at most as large as N, which can be shown by either surjecting N onto X or injecting X into N.
If X and Y are countably infinite sets, then X × Y is countably infinite.
Let n ≥ 1 and let X1, ..., Xn be countably infinite sets. Then the product ∏i=1n Xi is countably infinite.
The set of all finite subsets of a countable set X is countable.
The set N × Z × Q is countably infinite.
The set of integers Z is countably infinite.
The set of all positive integers is countably infinite.
The set of all even natural numbers is countably infinite, and the set of all odd natural numbers is countably infinite.
The set P(N) is uncountable; intuitively, the infinite subsets of N cannot be expressed finitely in a uniform way.
The set R is uncountable; intuitively, there is no uniform way of finitely describing real numbers—for example, decimal expansions are no good since they are infinite.
There exist sets X and Y of different cardinalities that have the same number of countably infinite subsets.
A set is countable if each of its elements has a finite description.
We often just want to know whether a set is countable, rather than countably infinite.

We made some progress in comparing the sizes of infinite sets, but only to a certain extent: at this point, we can only distinguish between two sizes of infinity, namely 'countable' and 'uncountable'.
An uncountable set is a set that is not countable, meaning it is neither finite nor countably infinite.
The existence of such sets is established by the fact that the power set of the natural numbers is uncountable.

Other sets identified as uncountable include the set of real numbers, the set of all functions from the natural numbers to the set {0, 1}, and the set of all functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers.
Intuitively, these sets are 'too big' for their elements to be listed, and their elements cannot be expressed finitely in a uniform way.
To prove that a set is uncountable, one can relate it to other sets already known to be uncountable.
Specifically, a set X is uncountable if there exists a surjection from X to an uncountable set U, or if there exists an injection from an uncountable set U into X.
These criteria allow for the detection of uncountability without relying solely on direct diagonal arguments.
Cantor's diagonal argument is a strategy used to prove that a set is uncountable.

It is a typical method for establishing uncountability, as demonstrated in the proof of the theorem concerning the uncountability of the set of all functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers.
The argument is also applied to prove that the set of real numbers is uncountable by utilizing decimal expansions.

In a specific application, the argument applies when a set B is defined as the set of natural numbers k such that k is not in f(k), which forces the condition that n is in B if and only if n is not in f(n) to hold for all natural numbers n.

While the argument is a direct method for proving uncountability, it can be cumbersome to use repeatedly; therefore, sets can also be proven uncountable by relating them to other sets that are already known to be uncountable.
The argument is distinct from Cantor's theorem, which implies that there is no bound on how large a cardinal number can be, and from the Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem.
The natural numbers are the nonnegative whole numbers.
Geometrically, they are represented by points on the number line obtained by starting at 0 and moving right by a whole unit length any number of times.
They can be described by the rules ( | 0 ) and ( n | n + 1 ), where ( | 0 ) means 0 is a natural number, and ( n | n + 1 ) means that if n is a natural number, then n + 1 is also a natural number.

According to the Peano axioms, every natural number is either 0 or the successor of a unique natural number; thus, every element can be obtained by starting from 0 and applying the successor operation ('plus one') a finite number of times.
In set theory, natural numbers can be encoded as sets known as von Neumann natural numbers.
In this construction, the natural number 0 is identified with the empty set ∅ (0 vN = ∅), and the successor operation s is defined as s(n vN) = n + vN for all n vN in the set N vN.
Natural numbers are closed under addition and multiplication, meaning that if a and b are natural numbers, then a + b and ab are also natural numbers.
However, they are not closed under subtraction or division.
While this text adopts the convention that natural numbers start at 0, some authors define them as positive whole numbers starting at 1.
Integers are the whole numbers, denoted by the set Z.
They can be represented as points on a number line obtained by starting at 0 and moving in either direction by the unit length any number of times.
Every integer is a rational number.
Integers are closed under addition, subtraction, and multiplication; if a and b are integers, then a + b, a - b, and ab are also integers.
However, this closure does not apply to division.
Integers can be used to measure the difference between two natural numbers.
The set Z is countable, as every integer has a finite description consisting of a finite string of digits, which may be modified by a minus sign.
A rational number is a real number that can be expressed as a fraction where the numerator is an integer and the denominator is a nonzero integer.
x is a rational number if and only if there exist integers a and b, with b ≠ 0, such that x = a/b.
The set of all rational numbers is denoted by Q.
This set is countable and forms a field, meaning that rational numbers can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided.
Every integer is a rational number.

For any two rational numbers x and y, the results of x + y, x - y, and xy are also rational numbers; furthermore, x/y is a rational number provided that y ≠ 0.
For a positive integer b, the real number 1/b represents the length obtained by dividing the unit length into b equal parts.
Real numbers are the numbers represented by points on the real number line, which consists of an infinite line with a fixed zero point and a fixed unit length.
The real numbers ( R, 0, 1, +, ·, ⩽ ) form a complete ordered field.
In the Dedekind reals approach, real numbers are identified with particular subsets of Q, where a real number r is identified with the set of rational numbers less than r.

Set-builder notation is a method of specifying a set by defining the properties that its elements must satisfy.

The notation is written as { x | p(x) }, where p(x) is a statement involving a variable x.
This expression denotes the set of all mathematical objects x that make the statement p(x) true.

An object a is considered an element of the set { x | p(x) } if and only if the property p(x) is true when a is substituted for x in the expression; symbolically, a ∈ { x | p(x) } if and only if p(a) is true.

While the comprehension axiom implies that anything defined using set-builder notation { x | p(x) } is a set, it is noted that one cannot simply write any expression in set-builder notation and expect it to be a set, as seen in the case of S = { X | X is a set }.

A proposition is a statement to which it makes sense to assign a truth value, which must be either true or false and cannot be both.
Propositions can be simple or complex.
Simpler propositions can be replaced with symbols called propositional variables (such as P, Q, or R) to examine the logical structure of a more complex proposition.

A truth table of a propositional formula is a table used to determine the truth values of the formula and its components.

It consists of one row for every possible assignment of truth values to the constituent propositional variables and one column for each subformula, which includes the propositional variables and the propositional formula itself.
The entries within the table are the truth values of these subformulae.
To construct a truth table for a complex formula, the truth tables for individual logical operators are combined.
This is achieved by examining the relevant columns located further to the left and comparing them with the truth table for the specific operator being applied.
Truth tables are used to streamline the process of proving logical equivalence.
Two formulas are considered logically equivalent if and only if they have the same truth values for all assignments of truth values to their constituent propositional variables.
Using truth tables can be a less painful alternative to proving equivalence through long strings of equations or double containment.
A tautology is a logical formula or proposition that remains true regardless of how truth values are assigned to its predicates and component propositional variables.
In symbolic logic, this is a precise definition and can be viewed as the opposite of a contradiction.
Examples of tautologies include the law of excluded middle, expressed as p ∨ ( ¬ p ), and the formula p ≅ ( q ≅ p ).
if q can be derived from p, then p ≅ q is a tautology; this is established by the introduction rule for implication (≅ I).
if p ≅ q is a tautology, then q can be derived from p by using the elimination rule for implication (≅ E) and the tautological assumption that p ≅ q is true.
Tautologies may be assumed in any proof of p.
in the context of the Lindenbaum-Tarski algebra over P, the relation ⊢ on A is defined such that [ s ] ⊢ [ t ] if and only if s ≅ t is a tautology.
A contradiction is a proposition that is known or assumed to be false.
In symbolic logic, the symbol ⊥ is used to represent a contradiction.
Examples of contradictions include assertions such as 0 = 1, the claim that √2 is rational, or the assertion that the equation x^2 = -1 has a solution x ∈ R.
If a contradiction is assumed, any consequence may be derived.
A contradiction is also reached if an assumption in a proof has the form ¬p and a derivation of p is subsequently obtained.
Contradiction is used as a basis for proof by contradiction.
In this process, one assumes the negation of the statement to be proven (or assumes a specific state) and derives a contradiction to prove the original statement.

To prove a statement of the form ∀n ⩾ n0, p(n), one may assume it is false, which implies the existence of a counterexample; proving that the set of all counterexamples has infinite descent leads to the desired contradiction.
In symbolic logic, a contradiction is considered the opposite of a tautology.

A predicate is a symbol p together with a specified list of free variables x1, x2, ..., xn (where n is a natural number) and, for each free variable xi, a specification of a set Xi called the range or domain of discourse of xi.
To make the variables explicit, a predicate is typically written as p(x1, x2, ..., xn).
Predicates represent statements that become propositions when specific values from their respective domains of discourse are substituted for their free variables.
A predicate with no free variables is precisely a propositional variable, meaning the notion of a predicate generalizes that of a propositional variable.
The universal quantifier, denoted by the symbol ∀, is one of the two main quantifiers used in mathematics.
It is used to make precise the meaning of phrases such as 'for all' or the statement that a logical formula p(x) is always true regardless of the value x takes.
If p(x) is a logical formula with a free variable x that has a range X, the universal quantifier is expressed as ∀x ∈ X, p(x).
The rule for universal introduction (∀ I) states that if p(x) can be derived from the assumption that x is an arbitrary element of X, then ∀x ∈ X, p(x).
The existential quantifier, denoted by the symbol ∃, is one of the two main quantifiers used in mathematics and is associated with the phrase 'there exists'.
An existentially quantified statement is established if there is at least one element in a set that satisfies a given property.
Specifically, if an element a is in set X and the property p(a) is true, then the statement ∃ x ∈ X, p(x) is true.
This quantifier is used to express that a property is satisfied by at least one object.
stating that a polynomial f(x) has a real root is equivalent to the existentially quantified statement ∃ x ∈ R, f(x) = 0.
In the context of logical formulae—which are expressions built from predicates using logical operators and quantifiers—variables can be either free or bound.
A variable x, understood to refer to an element of a set X, is considered free if it makes sense to substitute particular elements of X into the statement.
If such substitution does not make sense, the variable is bound.
Variables are turned from free into bound by expressions that refer to how many elements of a set make a statement true, such as the words 'every' and 'there exists'.
in the expression 'there exist integers a and b such that x = a2 + b2', x is a free variable while a and b are bound variables.
in the expression 'every even natural number n ≥ 2 is divisible by k', k is the free variable and n is the bound variable.
The truth value of a logical formula depends on its free variables, according to the rules for logical operators and quantifiers.
Logical equivalence, denoted by the symbol ≡, is an equivalence relation on the set of all logical formulae (specifically on L(P)).
It captures the sense in which two logical formulae 'mean the same thing.'
For propositional formulae, two formulae are logically equivalent if and only if their truth values are the same under any assignment of truth values to their constituent propositional variables.
In a truth table, this is evidenced by the formulae having identical columns.

Proving logical equivalence can be achieved through several methods: 1. Direct use of the definition of logical equivalence. 2. Using truth tables to check if the formulae are true and false in a list of cases. 3. Applying known logical equivalences, such as the law of double negation.
Logical equivalence is used to transform a logical formula into a different but equivalent form, which allows for the identification of a wider range of feasible proof strategies.

De Morgan's laws describe a duality between conjunction (∧) and disjunction (∨), and are used as rules for negating these operators.
These laws exist in a general version for Boolean algebras, which implies specific versions for logical formulae and for sets (specifically the set operations of union and intersection).
In the context of Boolean algebras, where ( X, ≼ ) is a Boolean algebra and x, y ∈ X, the laws involve the relation z = ( ¬ x ) ∨ ( ¬ y ).
De Morgan's laws for logical operators generalize to statements about quantifiers, expressing a duality between the universal quantifier (∀) and the existential quantifier (∃).

The cartesian product is an operation used to construct sets of ordered lists.
In these lists, the sets involved in the product determine the type of object that can occupy the corresponding term in the list.
An indexed cartesian product of a family of sets { Xi | i ∈ I } indexed by a set I is defined.

Intuitively, this is constructed by devising a step-by-step procedure for specifying an element of X, represented by the formula n ∏ k = 1 Xk, where Xk is the set of choices to be made in the k th step.
Elements of cartesian products do not depend on one another.
Consequently, a set of sequences of choices cannot be expressed as a cartesian product if the choices available in one step depend on the choice made in a previous step.
The axiom of choice states that the cartesian product of every family of inhabited sets is inhabited.
The cardinality of the cartesian product is referred to as the cardinal product (or indexed cardinal product in the case of indexed cartesian products).
An indexed family of sets over a set I is a specification of a set Ai for each element i in I.
