Because surveys allow researchers to collect data from very large samples for a relatively low cost, survey methods lend themselves to probability sampling techniques.
Survey research is probably the best method to use when one hopes to gain a representative picture of the attitudes and characteristics of a large group.
Survey research tends to be a reliable method of inquiry.
Surveys are standardized in that the same questions, phrased in exactly the same way, are posed to participants.
Qualitative approaches do not offer the same consistency that a quantitative survey offers.
A poorly phrased question can cause respondents to interpret its meaning differently, which can reduce that question’s reliability.
The versatility of survey research is also an asset.
Surveys are used by all kinds of people in all kinds of professions.
Understanding how to construct and administer surveys is a useful skill to have for all kinds of jobs.

Lawyers might use surveys in their efforts to select juries, social service and other organizations (e.g., churches, clubs, fundraising groups, activist groups) use them to evaluate the effectiveness of their efforts, businesses use them to learn how to market their products, governments use them to understand community opinions and needs, and politicians and media outlets use surveys to understand their constituencies.
Survey research also comes with a few drawbacks.

While one might argue that surveys are flexible in the sense that we can ask any number of questions on any number of topics in them, the fact that the survey researcher is generally stuck with a single instrument for collecting data (the questionnaire), surveys are in many ways rather inflexible.

If a researcher mails a survey out to 1,000 people and then discovers, as responses start coming in, that the phrasing on a particular question seems to be confusing a number of respondents, it is too late for a do-over or to change the question for the respondents who haven’t yet returned their surveys.

When conducting in-depth interviews, on the other hand, a researcher can provide respondents further explanation if they’re confused by a question and can tweak their questions as they learn more about how respondents seem to understand them.
Validity can also be a problem with surveys.
It can be difficult to ask anything other than very general questions that a broad range of people will understand.
Survey results may not be as valid as results obtained using methods of data collection that allow a researcher to more comprehensively examine whatever topic is being studied.

If a researcher wants to learn something about voters’ willingness to elect an African American president, General Social Survey respondents were asked, “If your party nominated an African American for president, would you vote for him if he were qualified for the job?”
Respondents were then asked to respond either yes or no to the question.
But what if someone’s opinion was more complex than could be answered with a simple yes or no?
What if, for example, a person was willing to vote for an African American woman but not an African American man?
Surveys are categorized by two primary dimensions: time (when or with what frequency they are administered) and administration (how they are delivered to respondents).
In terms of time, there are two main types: cross-sectional and longitudinal.
Cross-sectional surveys are administered at a single point in time, providing a snapshot of respondents' attitudes or behaviors at that specific moment.
A limitation of cross-sectional surveys is that they capture a static moment, making it difficult to determine if the observed phenomena remain stable over time.
Longitudinal surveys, in contrast, enable researchers to make observations over an extended period, allowing them to capture changes in behavior or phenomena caused by world events or aging.
There are several types of longitudinal surveys, including trend, panel, and cohort surveys, as well as retrospective surveys.
Trend surveys focus on how people's inclinations change over time; the same individuals do not necessarily participate in each administration, provided the sample is representative of the population.
Panel surveys involve the same group of people being surveyed repeatedly over time.
Cohort surveys involve identifying a specific category of people and regularly surveying those who fall into that category.

Retrospective surveys are administered only once, like cross-sectional surveys, but ask participants to report on past events, allowing researchers to gather longitudinal-like data without the time and expense of a true longitudinal study.
The primary drawback of retrospective surveys is the potential for faulty recollections of past events.
In terms of administration, surveys can be self-administered or conducted as interviews.
Self-administered questionnaires are given to participants in writing to respond to on their own; these can be delivered in person, via mail, or online.
Interviews involve a researcher posing questions directly to respondents, collecting data through personal interaction.

The choice of administration method involves trade-offs: online surveys may be faster and cheaper but require respondents to have necessary hardware and internet access, while mailed surveys may reach a broader sample but are more likely to be lost or not returned.
Designing effective questions and questionnaires is the process of creating survey items that yield usable data and presenting them in a format that respondents can easily complete.

The process begins with identifying exactly what information is needed, which involves brainstorming, consulting the literature, and ranking questions to ensure the most important factors are included despite time or space limitations.

When writing individual questions, researchers must avoid wording that causes confusion, such as double negatives, culturally specific terms, or double-barreled questions that ask multiple things at once.
Survey questions must also be relevant to all respondents, using filter questions when necessary.

When creating response options, designers must balance the problem of fence-sitting (where respondents choose a neutral option) against the problem of floating (where respondents are unsure how to categorize their answer), as solving one issue may cause the other.
Pretesting is a critical step to improve the survey before administration.
The final stage involves designing the questionnaire itself, which is the document containing all questions.
This requires grouping questions thematically and determining the order of presentation.

While there is disagreement about where to place demographic questions, the order should generally be determined by the unique characteristics of the research and the needs of the respondents to maximize completion rates and credibility.
Analysis of survey data is the process of condensing large amounts of information from completed questionnaires into usable and understandable chunks.
The primary goal of this analysis is to identify, describe, and explain patterns in the data.
The process typically begins with data entry, where response options are coded numerically and entered into a data analysis computer program.
Researchers then run various statistical commands to identify patterns across responses.
Several computer programs are designed to assist survey researchers with this task, including SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences), MicroCase, and Excel.
SPSS is noted for its ability to perform both basic descriptive and complex inferential statistical analysis, while Excel is described as less sophisticated but relatively easy to use.
The most basic form of analysis is univariate analysis, in which researchers describe patterns across just one variable using frequency distributions and measures of central tendency.
When researchers are interested in simultaneously analyzing relationships among more than two variables, they conduct multivariate analysis.
Survey data are well suited to a deductive approach, allowing researchers to analyze data to test hypotheses generated based on theories.
While survey researchers should aim for the highest response rate possible, some recent research suggests that high return rates may be less important than previously thought.

A cross-sectional survey is a research instrument administered only once to capture a snapshot of life, events, opinions, behaviors, or other phenomena as they exist at the specific moment of administration.
This single-time-point design distinguishes it from longitudinal surveys, which enable researchers to make observations over an extended period of time to track changes.

The primary limitation of the cross-sectional approach is that the phenomena it assesses do not generally remain stagnant; while the survey can describe the state of the world at the moment of data collection, it is difficult to determine whether those conditions remained the same for long after the survey was administered.

For example, a survey asking for opinions on terrorism on September 10, 2001, would capture a specific moment in time, but it would not reveal how those opinions evolved in the days or weeks that followed.

The decision to use a cross-sectional survey is often driven by the prohibitive time and cost required to administer longitudinal surveys, making the single administration a practical alternative for gathering data.

Although longitudinal surveys are generally preferable for their ability to track changes over time, the cross-sectional design remains a standard method in survey research for assessing the current state of a population.
A longitudinal survey is a research design that enables a researcher to make observations over an extended period of time.
This approach is used to capture changes in behavior or other phenomena, whether those changes result from world events or from people aging.
The primary types of longitudinal surveys include trend, panel, and cohort surveys.

A trend survey focuses on how people's inclinations change over time; for example, Gallup opinion polls administer the same questions to people at different points in time to track shifts in public opinion, such as changing attitudes toward gas prices.
In trend surveys, it is not necessary for the same people to participate each time, provided the sample is representative of the population.
A cohort survey involves identifying a specific category of people and regularly surveying those who fall into that category.
While longitudinal surveys are preferable for tracking changes over time, they are distinguished from cross-sectional surveys by the frequency and timing of administration.
The main limitation of longitudinal surveys is that the time and cost required to administer them can be prohibitive.
Retrospective surveys are related but distinct; they deal with changes over time but are administered only once, asking participants to report past events.
This offers the benefit of longitudinal-like data without the expense, though it carries the drawback of potentially faulty recollections.
A retrospective survey is a research design in which participants are asked to report events, behaviors, beliefs, or experiences from the past.

It is classified as a type of longitudinal survey because it deals with changes over time, but it is distinct from other longitudinal designs because it is administered only once, similar to a cross-sectional study.

The primary purpose of a retrospective survey is to allow researchers to gather longitudinal-like data without incurring the time or expense associated with administering a survey over an extended period.
However, this approach involves a trade-off: the benefit of efficiency must be weighed against the possibility that participants' recollections of their pasts may be faulty.

The accuracy of these reports can vary depending on how far back in time the events occurred; for instance, recalling a recent event may be more accurate than recalling events from several years prior.
Retrospective surveys thus offer some of the benefits of longitudinal research but come with specific drawbacks related to memory reliability.
Response rate is a metric used in survey research to measure the proportion of questionnaires that are returned in a completed and readable format.
It is calculated by dividing the number of completed questionnaires received by the number of questionnaires distributed.
For example, if 75 out of 100 distributed questionnaires are returned completed, the response rate is 75%.
a rate of three-quarters (75%) is generally considered good or excellent by most survey researchers
There is significant research dedicated to improving survey response rates.
Fence-sitting and floating are two distinct issues in survey design related to how response options are structured.
Fence-sitting occurs when respondents choose neutral response options, such as 'no opinion,' even if they actually have an opinion.
This behavior can occur when respondents are given rank-ordered response options that include a neutral middle choice, such as a five-point scale ranging from strongly agree to strongly disagree.
Floating is described as the flip side of fence-sitting.
The decision of whether to allow fence-sitting or to force respondents to choose an opinion depends on the goals of the research.
In some cases, allowing fence-sitting is necessary, while in others, it may be acceptable to force respondents to choose an opinion.
There is a trade-off in creating response options: the solution to the problem of fence-sitting might cause floating, whereas the solution to the problem of floating might cause fence-sitting.
These concepts are part of the broader process of creating effective survey questions and response options.
Univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analysis are three levels of quantitative data analysis used to identify, describe, and explain patterns in survey data.
Univariate analysis is the most basic form, in which researchers describe patterns across just one variable; it includes frequency distributions and measures of central tendency.
Bivariate analysis assesses covariation among two variables, allowing researchers to determine whether changes in one variable occur together with changes in another.
If two variables do not covary, they are said to have independence.
A common procedure for bivariate analysis is to cross-tabulate the two variables and present their relationship in a contingency table.
Multivariate analysis involves simultaneously analyzing relationships among more than two variables.

if a researcher hypothesizes that financial security declines for women as they age but increases for men as they age, adding age to an analysis of gender and financial security would require multivariate rather than bivariate analysis.
The goal of these analyses is to condense large amounts of information into usable and understandable chunks, turning completed questionnaires into shareable findings.
Interview research is a methodological approach used to gather detailed information and examine processes.
It is particularly effective when the research topic is complex, when questions require lengthy explanation, or when participants need time and dialogue to work through their responses.
A key advantage of interviews over surveys is the ability to ask follow-up questions in real time, allowing researchers to explore the story behind initial responses.
This method is especially useful when researchers need to understand unique, individual narratives that cannot be captured by closed-ended survey questions.

For example, interviews are well-suited for studying complex decision-making processes, such as how individuals decide not to have children and how others respond to that decision, where back-and-forth dialogue is necessary to uncover the full context.

Qualitative interviews, also known as intensive or in-depth interviews, are semistructured interactions where the researcher guides a conversation to gather detailed information about a specific topic.
The primary aim is to hear from respondents about what they consider important regarding the topic, captured in their own words.
These interviews utilize open-ended questions, which do not provide answer options and require participants to formulate their own responses.
This approach contrasts with quantitative interviewing, which relies on rigid schedules and uniform probing to minimize interviewer effects.
Qualitative interviewing techniques are designed to go with the flow, allowing the interview to take the direction the respondent chooses.
To support this flexibility, researchers typically develop an interview guide in advance, which serves as a non-rigid list of topics or questions to cover.
A key technique in qualitative interviewing is active listening, where the researcher participates by showing understanding and following the respondent's narrative.
This often involves probing, defined as a request for more information, to encourage respondents to explain or describe their experiences further.
Researchers are advised to prepare helpful probes in advance and practice interviews with individuals similar to the sample to avoid being stumped during the interaction.

Considerations for qualitative interviewing include acknowledging the power differential between the researcher and the participant, selecting an appropriate location, and recognizing the interview as a form of relationship.
Interviewers must always be respectful of participants, a principle emphasized by feminist researchers who have helped balance power dynamics.

While qualitative interviews allow for deep understanding of social processes, they have drawbacks, including reliance on the accuracy of respondents and the intensity of the process in terms of time, expense, and potential emotional strain.
It is common for qualitative interviewers to take audio recordings of the interviews they conduct.

Quantitative interviews are a data collection method in which a researcher poses questions directly to respondents, typically using closed-ended questions delivered in the same format and order to every participant.
This approach distinguishes quantitative interviewing from qualitative interviewing, which is semistructured, uses open-ended questions, and allows the conversation to follow the respondent's lead.

In quantitative interviews, probing is uniform and often predetermined; interviewers are instructed to avoid probes that might appear to agree or disagree with the respondent, using neutral acknowledgments only when explicitly requested by the participant.
The primary aim of quantitative interviewing is to represent and condense data into numbers, allowing for statistical analysis.
Data analysis typically involves coding response options numerically, entering these values into a data analysis program, and running statistical commands to identify patterns.
Quantitative interviews offer advantages over self-administered questionnaires, such as the ability to clarify confusing items and potentially higher response rates.

However, they carry the drawback of interviewer effect, where the presence of a human administrator introduces variables that may influence responses, and they are generally more time-consuming and expensive than written surveys.

All interviewers, including those using quantitative techniques, must consider the power differential between themselves and respondents, choose appropriate interview locations, and maintain respect for participants.
The unit 'Issues to Consider for All Interview Types' addresses considerations that are relevant to both qualitative and quantitative interviewing.

It is distinguished from units focused on the unique features of specific approaches, such as qualitative or quantitative interview techniques, by its scope, which covers factors that apply to all interviewers regardless of the specific method used.
The evidence identifies two specific issues that fall under this category: where to conduct an interview and how to make participants as comfortable as possible during the interview.
All interviewers should be aware of, give some thought to, and plan for these additional factors.
These considerations are treated as distinct from the unique features of qualitative or quantitative approaches, which are addressed in separate sections of the source material.
An interview guide is a list of topics or questions that a researcher develops in advance to guide the interviewer during a qualitative interview.
It is not a rigid script; rather, it functions like an agenda or to-do list, allowing the interviewer to cover key areas while adapting to the participant's responses.
In qualitative interviewing, the guide outlines issues the researcher considers important, but the flow of the interview is shaped by the participant's own words and priorities.
The specific format of an interview guide can vary based on the interviewer's style and experience, ranging from a brief outline of topic headings to a detailed list of specific questions.

Researchers may create two versions of a guide: a detailed version for preparation and practice, and a brief outline to use during the actual interview to encourage active listening and avoid the impression that the interviewer is more interested in their questions than the participant's answers.
The construction of an interview guide is a deliberate process that typically begins with brainstorming all relevant topics and questions.
The researcher then refines this list by removing redundancies, grouping similar items, and creating thematic headings.
It is also recommended to consult scholarly literature to identify questions used in similar studies.
When ordering the guide, sensitive or controversial questions should generally be avoided at the beginning to allow participants to warm up.
The guide should primarily use open-ended questions to allow participants to share information in their own words.

Follow-up questions should be used to probe for more detail, but phrasing should be non-confrontational; for example, asking 'Could you tell me a little more about that?' is preferred over asking 'why,' which can feel hostile.
Finally, the guide should be reviewed for feedback to catch overlooked issues before data collection begins.
A standardized interview is a quantitative data collection method in which questions and answer options are read to respondents rather than having respondents complete a questionnaire on their own.
This approach distinguishes standardized interviews from surveys, which rely on self-administered questionnaires.
The questions posed in a standardized interview tend to be closed-ended, similar to those used in questionnaires.
However, there are instances in which a quantitative interviewer might pose a few open-ended questions as well.
In these cases, the coding process works somewhat differently than coding in-depth interview data.
The unit is situated within the broader context of quantitative interview techniques and considerations, and it is distinct from qualitative interview approaches.

A semi-structured interview is a qualitative research method, also referred to as an intensive or in-depth interview, in which the researcher has a particular topic in mind but uses open-ended questions that may not be asked in exactly the same way or in exactly the same order to each respondent.
The primary aim of this approach is to hear from respondents about what they think is important about the topic at hand and to hear it in their own words.

In practice, the interview often feels more like a conversation than a formal interview to the respondent, but the researcher is usually guiding the conversation with the goal of gathering information.
The researcher typically develops an interview guide in advance, which is a list of topics or questions to cover during the interview.
This guide is used to guide the interviewer but is not set in stone; it allows for flexibility in the order of questions and the specific wording used, depending on how the participant responds.
Semi-structured interviews are useful for gathering detailed information and understanding social processes, as they allow respondents to share information in their own words.
However, drawbacks include reliance on the accuracy of respondents and the intensity of the method in terms of time, expense, and possible emotional strain.

A focus group is a qualitative data collection method defined as a planned discussion designed to elicit group interaction and obtain perceptions on a defined area of interest in a permissive, nonthreatening environment.
Unlike one-on-one qualitative interviews, where the researcher primarily acts as a listener and question asker, focus groups are more dynamic and rely on the group interaction as a key focal point.
The researcher takes the role of a moderator, posing questions or topics for discussion and then allowing group members to discuss the question or topic among themselves.

Participants may ask each other follow-up questions, agree or disagree with one another, display body language that reveals their feelings about the conversation, or even come up with questions not previously conceived of by the researcher.
These interactions and displays are of direct interest to the researcher, who aims to get participants talking to each other and to observe interactions among participants.
Group size should be determined in part by the topic of the interview and the likelihood that participants will have much to say without much prompting.
If the topic is one about which participants feel passionately and will have much to say, a group of 3–5 is ideal.
Some recommend that a group of about 6–10 participants is the ideal size for focus group research.
In terms of focus group composition, homogeneity of background among participants is recommended while diverse attitudes within the group are ideal.
Focus groups share many of the strengths and weaknesses of one-on-one qualitative interviews.
Both methods can yield very detailed, in-depth information and provide researchers with an opportunity to observe participants' body language.
Focus groups offer the added benefit of giving researchers a chance to collect data on human interaction by observing how group participants respond and react to one another.
Focus groups can be expensive and time-consuming, though there may be some time savings as it takes fewer group events than one-on-one interviews to gather data from the same number of people.
A potential drawback of focus groups, which is not a concern for one-on-one interviews, is that one or two participants might dominate the group, silencing other participants.
Careful planning and skillful moderation on the part of the researcher are crucial for avoiding, or at least dealing with, such possibilities.

Focus groups are used in a variety of professions, from market research to academia to government and political research, and are a useful method for researchers who wish to gather in-depth information about social processes.
A probe is a request for more information used by interviewers to elicit additional details from respondents.
Probing is an active listening practice that supports rapport by demonstrating that the researcher understands and follows the respondent's narrative.
Both qualitative and quantitative interviewers use probes, though the methods differ.
In quantitative interviews, probing should be uniform, and interviewers often predetermine the types of probes they will use.
Quantitative interviewers are typically instructed to avoid probes that might signal agreement or disagreement with the respondent's statements.

In qualitative interviews, probing is more flexible and designed to follow the flow of the conversation, allowing the interviewer to ask respondents to explain, describe, or provide more information as the interview progresses.
Even in qualitative settings, it is recommended to prepare helpful probes in advance to avoid being unprepared when a respondent offers a topic that requires further exploration.
Field research is a qualitative method of data collection aimed at understanding, observing, and interacting with people in their natural settings.
In this context, being in 'the field' means being out in the real world and involved in the everyday lives of the people being studied.

Field research functions as an umbrella term that encompasses the myriad activities field researchers engage in when collecting data, typically involving a combination of participant observation, interviewing, and the analysis of documents or artifacts created by the people observed.
The method has its origins in anthropology, and researchers sometimes use the terms ethnography or participant observation to refer to this specific approach.
Field research is used when researchers seek to gain firsthand experience and knowledge about the people, events, and processes they study.
It provides a close-up lens on everyday life, allowing for the collection of very detailed data about people and processes, often more detailed than what can be obtained using other methods.
It is an excellent method for understanding the role of social context in shaping people’s lives and experiences, enabling a greater understanding of the intricacies and complexities of daily life.
A unique strength of field research is its ability to uncover elements of people’s experiences or group interactions of which researchers were not previously aware.

Unlike interviews and surveys, where respondents cannot provide information they are not aware of, field research typically occurs over an extended period of time, allowing social facts that may not be immediately revealed to be discovered over the course of the project.
Field research is a qualitative method that allows researchers to gain firsthand experience and knowledge about the people, events, and processes they study.
It provides a close-up lens on everyday life, enabling the collection of very detailed data about people and processes, potentially more detailed than other methods.

A unique strength of field research is its ability to uncover elements of people's experiences or group interactions that were not previously known, as well as social facts that emerge over time rather than being immediately revealed.
This method is particularly effective for understanding the role of social context in shaping lives and the intricacies of daily life.
It can be emotionally taxing for the researcher, often requiring a deep, committed relationship with participants that is more intensive than the relationship required in interview research.
Field researchers cannot be certain about the effect their presence may have on the people and interactions they observe.
The decision to enter the field as an overt or covert researcher also presents distinct pros and cons, with the chosen role affecting subsequent experiences in the field.
In the context of field research, 'getting in' refers to the process of entering a research site and establishing a role, which involves deciding where to observe and what role to take.
The two major considerations regarding this process are the choice between an overt or covert role and the practical and ethical implications of that choice.
As an overt researcher, one may experience initial difficulty establishing rapport, though having an insider who can vouch for the researcher helps.
However, the knowledge that subjects are being watched can make participants uncomfortable and cause them to behave differently than they would if unaware of being studied.
Because field research is typically a sustained activity occurring over several months or years, participants are likely to become more comfortable with the researcher's presence over time.
Overt researchers also avoid a variety of moral and ethical dilemmas that they might otherwise face.

In contrast, as a covert researcher, 'getting in' to the site might be easier, but this approach introduces other issues, such as the potential for participants to react negatively upon discovering they have been studied, or the researcher being asked to engage in activities they find unsettling or unsafe.

The decision to enter a field covertly is often influenced by factors beyond the researcher's personal comfort, including institutional review board (IRB) policies regarding deception and the extent to which the research site is a public location where people may not have an expectation of privacy.
Field notes are the first and necessary step toward developing quality analysis in field research, serving as the record that affirms what a researcher observed.

Writing field notes is a skill that can be improved with practice; conducting field research and taking field notes are decidedly not informal activities, and observation in field research is deliberate, not haphazard.
Understanding when to write, what to write, where to write, and how to write are all skills that field researchers develop with experience.
There are two different kinds of field notes: descriptive and analytic.

Descriptive field notes are notes that simply describe a field researcher’s observations as straightforwardly as possible; they typically do not contain explanations of or comments about those observations, and the observations are presented on their own, as clearly as possible.
Analytic field notes are notes that include the researcher’s impressions about their observations.
Writing and analyzing field notes involves moving from description to analysis.

Analyzing field note data is a process that occurs over time, beginning at the moment a field researcher enters the field and continuing as interactions are happening in the field, as the researcher writes up descriptive notes, and as the researcher considers what those interactions and descriptive notes mean.
Field researchers typically spend several hours typing up field notes after each observation has occurred.
Having time outside of the field to reflect upon thoughts about what has been seen and the meaning of those observations is crucial to developing analysis in field research studies.
Once the analytic field notes have been written or typed up, the field researcher can begin to look for patterns across the notes by coding the data.
The strategy for recording observations while in the field is determined mostly by the site chosen and the role played in that site.
Writing notes while in the field requires a fine balance between jotting down observations and actually engaging in the setting.
If a researcher is strictly an observer, these are easy to balance; but if also a participant, note taking should not keep the researcher from participating.

In locations where taking notes “in the moment” would be too obvious, rude, or distracting, a researcher may still occasionally jot down a few things very quickly, or develop a way of jotting down observations that doesn’t require complete sentences or perhaps even words.

Some field researchers have developed their own version of shorthand to take notes, using some combination of abbreviations and symbols, without taking too much time away from their participation in the field.

Field researchers use a variety of strategies to take notes while in the field, including jotting notes on their hands and arms, keeping very small notebooks in their pockets, carrying small recorders to make quick observations, and even writing notes on toilet paper during visits to the restroom.
With the advent of smartphones, taking notes in the field has become less arduous than it once was.
The aim is to record observations as straightforwardly and, while in the field, as quickly as possible in a way that makes sense to the researcher.
It is important to note as much as possible while in the field and as much as can be recalled after leaving the field because it is never known what might become important.
Things that seem decidedly unimportant at the time may later reveal themselves to have some relevance.

Details that may seem unimportant in the moment may turn out to be important during later analysis; it is therefore crucial that field researchers make note of these observations when conducting field research.

It is important that field researchers not allow their original question or topic to blind them to occurrences in the field that may not seem particularly important at the time, because it is never known whether or how some observation might be important down the line.

In one researcher’s field research experience, field notes included a number of direct quotes and descriptions of informal interactions with participants that were not expected to be important but were nevertheless jotted down.
Several of these quotes eventually made their way into the analysis.

For example, Polly, who ran the volunteer office for a breast cancer organization, once remarked that the office does not use disposable cups and that it is always best to have coffee in a real mug because it is much nicer for volunteers to drink out of a real mug instead of a disposable cup.

Because of this, Polly spends a large amount of time washing mugs every day and throughout the day so that a clean, real mug is always available to the many volunteers who show up for brief volunteer shifts at the office each day.

Had the researcher not made a note of the coffee cup interaction with Polly, which at the time seemed rather mundane, the researcher may have missed an important analytic point about the invisibility of some components of women’s volunteer labor that was later able to be made in presentations and publications of the work.
In analyzing their data, many field researchers conduct grounded theory.
Grounded theory involves generating theory from the ground up.
Analysis of field research data is the process of moving from raw descriptive observations to analytic insights that make sense to others.

This process is not a single event but occurs over time, beginning when a researcher enters the field and continuing as interactions happen, descriptive notes are written, and the researcher reflects on the meaning of those observations.
A key component of this analysis is the creation of analytic field notes, which are notes that include the researcher's impressions about their observations, distinct from purely descriptive notes.
The analysis typically begins immediately after exiting the field, where researchers spend several hours typing up messy jotted notes or recordings into a more readable format.
This period of reflection outside the field is crucial for developing analysis.
Once analytic field notes are written, the researcher begins to look for patterns across the notes by coding the data.
It is important to note as much as possible while in the field because things that seem unimportant at the time may later reveal themselves to have analytic relevance.

a researcher might note a mundane interaction, such as a volunteer office manager washing mugs to avoid disposable cups, which later becomes a key analytic point about the invisibility of certain types of labor.
This approach ensures that the detailed data collected through field research is transformed into meaningful findings.
Participant observation is a qualitative method of data collection that focuses on the participation and observation aspects of field research.
It is used to understand, observe, and interact with people in their natural settings, often referred to as being in 'the field.'

While field research is an umbrella term that includes interviewing and document or artifact analysis, participant observation specifically refers to the researcher's engagement in the everyday lives of the people they are studying.
The term is commonly used in sociology, whereas anthropology more frequently uses the term ethnography for similar methods.
A defining feature of participant observation is the continuum of roles a researcher can adopt, ranging from a complete observer to a complete participant.
Complete observers may miss important aspects of group interaction and the lived experience of the people they study, but they can see interactions that might be missed if they were more involved.

Complete participants gain a real taste of life in the group, which some argue is the only way to truly understand the subject, but they may face ethical quandaries, such as deceiving subjects, or find themselves in situations they cannot excuse themselves from.
In reality, most field research projects lie somewhere near the middle of this observer-participant continuum, where researchers participate to at least some extent but also observe.
The choice of role and site is often shaped by limitations such as time.
Field researchers typically immerse themselves in their research sites for many months or even years.
For example, one researcher conducted over 300 hours of participant observation over a period of 3 years.
The method is well-equipped to answer 'how' kinds of questions, such as how processes occur and how people interact, rather than the 'why' questions often targeted by survey research.
Field notes are a critical component, where researchers distinguish between what they actually observed and their reflections or thoughts about those observations.
This distinction helps in analyzing data and confronting personal biases.
Descriptive field notes are notes that simply describe a field researcher’s observations as straightforwardly as possible.
These notes typically do not contain explanations of or comments about those observations; instead, the observations are presented on their own, as clearly as possible.
This type of writing is not intended for literary value, interest, or readability for anyone other than the researcher.
The aim is to record observations as straightforwardly and, while in the field, as quickly as possible in a way that makes sense to the researcher.
Descriptive field notes serve as the first and necessary step toward developing quality analysis and act as the record that affirms what was observed.
Field researchers use a variety of strategies to take notes while in the field.
While some research is conducted in settings where sitting with a notebook, iPad, or computer is no problem, this is the exception rather than the norm.

More often, field researchers must find creative ways to note their observations while engaged in the field, such as jotting notes on their hands and arms, keeping very small notebooks in their pockets, dictating observations into a handheld recorder, or taking notes in the form of text messages on a phone.
When taking descriptive field notes, researchers should try to make note of their observations as straightforwardly as possible.

It is important to note as much as possible while in the field and as much as can be recalled after leaving the field, because things that seem unimportant at the time may later reveal themselves to have relevance.

Direct quotes may be difficult to remember, so researchers may write verbatim quotes while in the field and then describe the circumstances under which something was said later when writing up full notes.
Handwritten notes are typically typed up immediately upon leaving the field so that researchers can “fill in the blanks” in their brief notes taken while in the field.
Field researchers typically spend several hours typing up field notes after each observation has occurred.

This process often marks the beginning of the analysis of field research data, as having time outside of the field to reflect upon thoughts about what was seen and the meaning of those observations is crucial to developing analysis.

Early in a field research project, researchers may focus slightly more on describing the “lay of the land,” writing up very detailed descriptions of the locations observed and the people interacted with.
They might also draw a map or, if appropriate, take pictures of field sites.
This documentation of first impressions is helpful because descriptive details that become part of the everyday scene later may stop being noticed over time.
Analytic field notes are notes that include the researcher’s impressions about their observations.
They represent a stage in the process of moving from description to analysis, where field notes develop from a more descriptive state to an analytic state.
This transition typically occurs when a field researcher exits an observation period and spends time typing up messy jotted notes or recordings into a more readable format.
Having time outside of the field to reflect upon thoughts about what was seen and the meaning of those observations is crucial to developing analysis.
Analytic field notes differ from descriptive field notes, which simply describe observations as straightforwardly as possible without containing explanations or comments.
In analytic notes, the researcher actively engages with the data by noting impressions, which may include details that seemed unimportant in the moment but later reveal analytic relevance.
This process is part of the broader effort to analyze field research data, which involves looking for patterns across the notes by coding the data.
The distinction between descriptive and analytic notes is useful for thinking about how to write and interpret field notes, even though the lines between description and analysis can be fuzzy.
Analytic field notes are thus a necessary step toward developing quality analysis in field research studies.
Grounded theory is an analytic process used by field researchers and others who conduct inductive analysis.
The primary goal of employing a grounded theory approach is to generate theory.

The name of the method implies two key characteristics: first, that discoveries are made from the ground up, and second, that theoretical developments are grounded in a researcher’s empirical observations and a group’s tangible experiences.
Because the process is open in nature and lacks pre-existing hypotheses to guide the analysis, it can feel intimidating or out of control to researchers, who may experience frustration or angst.

However, developing a coherent theory grounded in empirical observations is considered rewarding for researchers, their peers who contribute to further theoretical development, and research participants who gain a broader view of their everyday experiences.
Grounded theory is a specific approach within the broader category of inductive qualitative data analysis.
Unobtrusive research refers to methods of collecting data that do not interfere with the subjects under study.
A defining characteristic of these methods is that they do not require the researcher to interact directly with the people being studied.

Instead, researchers analyze evidence of human behavior that people create or leave behind, such as letters to the editor, entertainment media, goods consumed, or physical traces like footprints on sidewalks.
Both qualitative and quantitative researchers use unobtrusive research methods.
Unobtrusive research is well suited to studies that focus on processes that occur over time or in the past.

Unlike longitudinal surveys or long-term field observations, unobtrusive methods enable researchers to investigate events and processes that have long since passed, without relying on retrospective accounts that may be subject to memory errors.

This approach is also well suited to comparative research, including historical comparative research that focuses on one or more cases over time or on more than one nation or society at one point in time.
Because researchers do not interact directly with participants, there is no possibility for the Hawthorne effect, which is the influence of the research process on the subjects' behavior.
Unobtrusive research is also relatively low-cost compared to other methods, as 'participants' are generally inanimate objects rather than human beings who must be compensated for their time.

Additionally, the method is forgiving: it is far easier to correct mistakes made in data collection than in interview, survey, or field research, because researchers can go back to the source of the data to gather more information or correct problems.
Because the data analyzed may have been created or gathered for purposes entirely different from the researcher's aim, problems of validity can arise.
Data sources measuring the specific phenomenon a researcher wishes to examine may simply not exist, forcing researchers to tweak their original research interests to suit available data.

Finally, it can be difficult to account for context; while unobtrusive research can provide a good understanding of what has occurred, it is often difficult to ascertain why something occurred, as the researcher cannot observe the events leading up to the occurrence or how people respond to it in real time.
Unobtrusive research is a method of collecting data that does not interfere with the subjects under study and does not require the researcher to interact directly with the people being studied.

this approach is well suited to examining processes that occur over time or in the past, and it allows researchers to investigate events that have long since passed without relying on retrospective accounts that may be subject to memory errors.
The strengths of unobtrusive research include the absence of the Hawthorne effect, which is the concern that a researcher's presence or interaction alters the behavior of participants.
unobtrusive researchers do not interact directly with their subjects, they do not need to be concerned about this specific type of research effect.

the method is relatively low-cost compared to other research methods because it often involves accessing data without paying human participants for their time, although travel or access to archives can still be costly.

Unobtrusive research is also considered 'forgiving' because it is easier to correct mistakes made during data collection than in other methods; researchers can return to the source of the data to gather more information or correct problems, a prospect that is not available in field research or survey research where the data collection campaign may be over.
The weaknesses of unobtrusive research include problems of validity, as the data analyzed may have been created or gathered for purposes entirely different from the researcher's aim.

Data sources measuring the specific phenomenon a researcher wishes to examine may simply not exist, forcing the researcher to tweak their original research interests or questions to suit the available data.
it can be difficult to account for context in unobtrusive research projects.

Unlike field research, where a researcher can observe the events leading up to an occurrence and how people respond, unobtrusive research makes it difficult to ascertain why something occurred, even if it provides a good understanding of what has occurred.

Unobtrusive data collected by the researcher refers to the analysis of texts, physical traces, or material artifacts that humans have left behind, such as worn paths, landfills, sculptures, or kitchen utensils.
This approach is distinct from observing people in person, which would no longer be unobtrusive, and from analyzing data collected by others.
The primary instrument used to record observations of these physical items is a code sheet, also known as a tally sheet in quantitative coding.
Once a set of artifacts is identified, the researcher must determine procedures for coding, distinguish between manifest and latent content, and identify patterns across the coded data.
Because many sources of unobtrusive data differ dramatically from written documents, standard open and focused coding may be less effective than using a code sheet to record specific details.

A code sheet can contain both qualitative and quantitative data; for example, a researcher might record the price of an item as a quantitative variable and their impressions of its ease of use as a qualitative note.
The aim of coding, whether the data are quantitative or qualitative, is to identify patterns across the coded data.

This method is cost-effective and allows for easier correction of mistakes than other data collection methods, as the researcher can return to the source to gather more information or correct problems in the original collection.
Analyzing Others' Data is a component of unobtrusive research in which a researcher analyzes existing data sets rather than collecting new data.
A key advantage of this approach is that the data collection phase can be skipped entirely.
The unit covers the use of publicly available quantitative and qualitative data sources.
For quantitative data, the General Social Survey (GSS) is a commonly used source, with data collected regularly since 1972 to investigate changes in Americans' attitudes and beliefs over time.
The GSS covers a broad range of topics, including family life, political and religious beliefs, and work experiences.

For researchers studying social processes outside the United States, the British Household Panel Study is a longitudinal, representative survey of households in Britain, freely available to academic researchers but charged for private entities.
The International Social Survey Programme merges the GSS with counterparts in other countries.
Other sources include the Center for Demography of Health and Aging, the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, the Carolina Population Center, and the National Opinion Research Center.
These represent a snapshot of the many sources of publicly available data accessible via the web.
Computer programs such as SPSS, MicroCase, and Excel are used to assist in analyzing this data.
SPSS is designed for quantitative survey data and can perform descriptive and inferential statistical analysis.
MicroCase includes similar features, while Excel is less sophisticated but easier to use.
The unit also notes that researchers taking a deductive approach study what others have done, read existing theories, and test hypotheses that emerge from those theories.

Reliability in unobtrusive research refers to the specific challenges and considerations involved in establishing the consistency and dependability of data coding within unobtrusive research projects.
This area of inquiry focuses on the mechanics of how and by whom data is coded, addressing the unique problems and opportunities that arise in this context.
The evaluation of reliability in this setting is structured around three core dimensions: stability, reproducibility, and accuracy.
Stability is a potential issue in unobtrusive research when the results of coding by the same person vary across different time periods.
Reproducibility concerns the extent to which multiple coders produce the same results when analyzing the same text.
Accuracy refers to the degree to which one’s coding procedures correspond to some preexisting standard.
These dimensions collectively define the framework for assessing reliability in unobtrusive research, distinguishing it from general methodological strengths or weaknesses of the approach.

Historical-comparative research is a methodological approach that focuses either on one or more cases over time (the historical part) or on more than one nation or society at one point in time (the comparative part).

This approach is characterized as unobtrusive, meaning it involves methods of collecting data that do not interfere with the subjects under study and do not require the researcher to interact with the people being studied.
Sociologists interested in history are likely to use these unobtrusive methods, which are also well suited to comparative research.
The method allows researchers to examine changes in multiple cases over time or to compare more than one nation or society at a single point in time without direct interaction with the subjects.
Content analysis is a method of unobtrusive research used to gather data by studying human communications.
It can be conducted qualitatively or quantitatively, and researchers often use both strategies to strengthen their investigations.
In qualitative content analysis, the aim is to identify themes in the text being analyzed and to identify the underlying meaning of those themes.
The texts that content analysts analyze include actual written texts such as newspapers or journal entries as well as visual and auditory sources such as television shows, advertisements, or movies.
Content analysts most typically analyze primary sources, though in some instances they may analyze secondary sources.
Primary sources represent the “raw” materials of history, while secondary sources are the “cooked” analyses of those materials.
Indirect measures that content analysts examine include physical traces and material artifacts.
Manifest content is apparent; latent content is underlying.
Content analysts use code sheets to collect data.
Ferree and Hall (1990) conducted a content analysis of introductory sociology textbooks, but their aim was not to learn about the content of sociology as a discipline.
Instead, the researchers sought to learn how students are taught the subject of sociology and understand what images are presented to students as representative of sociology as a discipline.
A graduate student colleague of the author once conducted qualitative content analysis in her study of national identity in the United States.
Other examples include a content analysis of women's portrayals in James Bond films and a video game character content analysis focused on hypersexuality.
Researcher bias is a risk inherent to all research projects, including unobtrusive research, where the researcher's presence or approach may influence the work.

It is distinct from the Hawthorne effect, which specifically refers to the effect of research on subjects and is not a concern for unobtrusive researchers who do not interact directly with participants.
The source notes that social constructionists and postmodernists might point out that bias is always a part of research to at least some degree.
The job of researchers is to recognize and address their biases as part of the research process, acknowledging it as an imperfect part of the work.
Researchers use particular approaches, such as theories, levels of analysis, or temporal processes, to frame and conduct their work.

Understanding these frames and approaches is crucial for successfully embarking upon and completing any research-based investigation, as well as for responsibly reading and understanding others' work.

Theories, paradigms, levels of analysis, and the order in which one proceeds in the research process all play an important role in shaping what we ask about the social world, how we ask it, and in some cases, even what we are likely to find.

One's theoretical perspective will also shape a study, with the theory invoked likely shaping not only the way a question about a topic is asked but also which topic gets investigated in the first place.
This does not mean that social science is biased or corrupt, but rather that bias is a recognized aspect of the research process that must be managed.
The Hawthorne effect is a phenomenon in research where subjects alter their behaviors because they know they are being studied.

This effect is a specific risk in research methods that involve direct interaction with participants, such as interviews, surveys, and field observations, where the presence of the researcher may influence the people and interactions being observed.
the Hawthorne effect is not a concern for unobtrusive research because these methods do not involve direct interaction with research participants.
This distinction is considered a major strength of unobtrusive research, as it allows researchers to avoid the behavioral changes induced by the awareness of being studied.
Primary and secondary sources are two distinct categories of data used in research, particularly in content analysis.
Primary sources are defined as the 'raw' materials of history, representing the original data or communications that have not yet been analyzed.
In contrast, secondary sources are those that have already been analyzed, often described as the 'cooked' analyses of those raw materials.
In the context of content analysis, researchers most typically analyze primary sources, though they may analyze secondary sources in specific instances.

When secondary sources are the focus of analysis, the researcher's interest usually lies in the process by which the original analyst reached their conclusions or the choices made in presenting the data.
This distinction is separate from a literature review, where researchers analyze secondary materials to understand the current state of knowledge on a topic.
The texts analyzed in content analysis can include written materials like newspapers and journal entries, as well as visual and auditory sources such as television shows, advertisements, and movies.
Physical traces are a form of unobtrusive data consisting of evidence left behind by humans that reveals information about their identities, behaviors, or actions.
They are distinct from material artifacts, which are objects created to communicate beliefs, values, or norms.
Examples of physical traces include worn paths across a campus, materials found in landfills or trash cans, indentations in furniture, and empty shelves in a grocery store.
In contrast, material artifacts include items such as video games, sculptures, mementos, housing structures, and kitchen utensils.
Physical traces are one of two primary methods for gathering data unobtrusively, the other being the content analysis of existing texts.

Analyzing these traces presents specific challenges because researchers generally lack access to the individuals who created them, and contacting them would violate the unobtrusive nature of the method.
Furthermore, interpreting the meaning of traces from different historical or cultural contexts can lead to validity and reliability issues.
To address this, researchers must understand who caused the trace, when it was created, why it was created, and for whom it was created.
This process may require accessing historical documents or using other data collection methods, such as interviews with creators, for contemporary items.
Once a set of physical traces is identified, the analysis involves determining coding procedures, distinguishing between manifest and latent content, and identifying patterns across the coded data.
Because standard note-taking may be ineffective for physical objects, researchers often use a code sheet or tally sheet to record observations systematically.
In the context of unobtrusive research, reliability is a matter of consistency, and it is evaluated through three specific dimensions: stability, reproducibility, and accuracy.
These dimensions address the unique problems and opportunities associated with how and by whom data coding occurs.
Stability refers to the extent to which the results of coding vary across different time periods.
Coding is considered stable when the same content is coded multiple times by the same person with the same result each time.
Problems with stability can arise from ambiguous coding rules, ambiguities in the text itself, or simple coding errors, such as inadvertently recording a 1 instead of a 10.
Reproducibility, sometimes referred to as intercoder reliability, is the extent to which coding procedures result in the same results when the same text is coded by different people.
Issues with reproducibility may stem from cognitive differences among coders, ambiguous coding instructions, or random coding errors.

One method for overcoming reproducibility problems is to have coders code together at the same time in the same room, allowing them to consult one another and develop a shared understanding of how to code various bits of data.
Accuracy refers to the extent to which one’s coding procedures correspond to some preexisting standard.

Focus groups are a qualitative data collection method defined as planned discussions designed to elicit group interaction and obtain perceptions on a defined area of interest in a permissive, nonthreatening environment.

Unlike one-on-one qualitative interviews, where the researcher typically acts as a listener and question asker to a single participant, focus groups are more dynamic and involve multiple respondents participating simultaneously.
The researcher takes the role of a moderator, posing questions or topics for discussion and then allowing group members to interact with one another.
The primary aim of this method is to get participants talking to each other and to observe the interactions among them, as the group interaction itself is a key focal point of the data collected.

In a focus group, participants may ask each other follow-up questions, agree or disagree with one another, display body language that reveals their feelings about the conversation, or even raise questions that the researcher had not previously conceived of.
Because of the nature and unpredictability of group interaction, focus groups tend to be qualitative rather than quantitative.

This method is useful for researchers who wish to gather in-depth information about social processes and offers the added benefit of collecting data on human interaction by observing how participants respond and react to one another.
Focus groups are used in a variety of professions, including market research, academia, and government and political research.
When forming focus groups, the number of participants typically ranges from 3 to 12.

The specific size of the group should be determined by considering the topic, the participants' potential interest and feelings about the topic, and the researcher's comfort level and experience in conducting focus groups.

While focus groups share many strengths and weaknesses with one-on-one qualitative interviews—such as the ability to yield detailed, in-depth information and the expense and time required—they offer the unique advantage of observing group dynamics.

A potential drawback specific to focus groups is that one or two participants might dominate the group, silencing others; careful planning and skillful moderation are crucial for managing this possibility.
There are also unique ethical concerns associated with collecting data in a group setting.
An experiment is a method of data collection designed to test hypotheses under controlled conditions.
It is most commonly a quantitative research method used to observe the consequences of specific actions or stimuli.
In social scientific research, the term has a unique meaning and should not be used to describe all research methodologies.
Designs considered to be 'true experiments' contain three key features: independent and dependent variables, pretesting and posttesting, and experimental and control groups.

In the classic experiment, the effect of a stimulus is tested by comparing two groups: one that is exposed to the stimulus (the experimental group) and another that does not receive the stimulus (the control group).
The effects of an independent variable upon a dependent variable are tested.

Because the researcher's interest lies in the effects of an independent variable, participants must be measured on the dependent variable before and after the independent variable (or stimulus) is administered.
Thus pretesting and posttesting are both important steps in a classic experiment.
In the Solomon four-group design, four groups exist.
Two groups are treated as they would be in a classic experiment.
Another group receives the stimulus and is then given the posttest.
The remaining group does not receive the stimulus but is given the posttest.
Experiments do not necessarily need to take place in the controlled setting of a lab.
Many applied researchers rely on experiments to assess the impact and effectiveness of various programs and policies.
In these applied settings, researchers apply their stimulus to some subjects in the field and have a control group in the field that does not receive the stimulus.

A strength of this method, particularly in cases where experiments are conducted in lab settings, is that the researcher has substantial control over the conditions to which participants are subjected.
Experiments are also generally easier to replicate than are other methods of data collection.
A disadvantage of experiments is that they are rather artificial.
Experiments that are conducted in applied settings may not be as subject to artificiality, though then their conditions are less easily controlled.
Experiments also present unique concerns regarding validity.
Problems of external validity might arise when the conditions of an experiment don’t adequately represent those of the world outside the boundaries of the experiment.
Concerns about internal validity also arise in experimental designs.

These have to do with the level of confidence about whether the stimulus actually produced the observed effect or whether some other factor, such as other conditions of the experiment or changes in participants over time, may have produced the effect.
True experimental designs differ from preexperimental designs, and preexperimental designs each lack one of the core features of true experimental designs.

Ethnomethodology and conversation analysis are unique approaches to analyzing qualitative data that rest upon particular ontological and epistemological assumptions, setting them apart from more traditional mechanisms of analysis such as coding.
Conversation analysis grew out of ethnomethodology and shares its focus on the construction of reality as opposed to the discovery of reality.

Conversation analysts focus specifically on talk in interaction: how talk progresses, how it is facilitated or impeded, how turns are taken in talk, and how these processes both shape and are shaped by social context.
In conversation analysis, what people say is just as important as how they say it.
Also important are the pauses people take in expressing themselves and how or whether they interrupt themselves or others while talking.
Conversation analysts might study recordings of court proceedings or legislative debates to learn about the social construction of law and punishment.
They might also study more simple interactions, such as a conversation between two people meeting for coffee.
An experiment is a method of data collection designed to test hypotheses under controlled conditions.

It is a quantitative research strategy used to observe the consequences of specific actions or stimuli, and the term has a unique meaning in social scientific research that distinguishes it from general empirical research projects.

In a classic experiment, the effect of a stimulus is tested by comparing an experimental group exposed to the stimulus with a control group that does not receive it.
Because the researcher's interest lies in the effects of an independent variable, participants must be measured on the dependent variable before and after the independent variable is administered.

In addition to the classic design, the Solomon four-group design is considered a true experiment; it involves four groups where two are treated as in a classic experiment, one receives the stimulus and a posttest, and the remaining group does not receive the stimulus but is given a posttest.
Experiments do not necessarily need to take place in a controlled lab setting; applied researchers often use them in the field to assess the impact and effectiveness of programs and policies.
Experiments enable researchers to have great control over conditions and are typically easier to replicate than other methods of data collection.
However, experiments come with some degree of artificiality and may run into problems of external or internal validity.

External validity problems arise when the conditions of an experiment do not adequately represent the world outside the experiment, while internal validity concerns the confidence that the stimulus, rather than other factors, produced the observed effect.
Internal validity is a concern that arises specifically in experimental designs.

It refers to the level of confidence researchers have about whether the stimulus actually produced the observed effect, or whether some other factor—such as other conditions of the experiment or changes in participants over time—may have produced the effect.
This concept is distinct from external validity, which concerns whether the conditions of an experiment adequately represent the world outside the boundaries of the experiment.
Experiments are designed to test hypotheses under controlled conditions, enabling researchers to have great control over the conditions to which participants are subjected.
However, because experiments come with some degree of artificiality, they may run into problems of internal validity.
Researchers must be aware that internal validity problems can occur and be forthcoming in their reports of findings about this potential weakness.

Ethnomethodologists study everyday reality and how people produce those realities through their presentations of self and interactions with others.
The discipline is often presented alongside conversation analysis in research methods texts, as both represent distinct approaches to qualitative data analysis.
