Different criteria can prefer different thresholds, meaning the selection is not unique but depends on the evaluation metric or objective used
The choice of this threshold has practical meaning in the application of the model

The threshold effect on precision, recall, and F1 describes how changing the score threshold of a classifier alters the set of predicted positives, thereby shifting the values of precision and recall.
A lower threshold results in more instances being predicted as positive.
As the score threshold increases, the number of predicted positives can stay the same or decrease.
At the lowest threshold, where every instance is labeled as positive, recall is 1, while precision equals the overall fraction of positives in the dataset.
As the threshold rises, precision may increase or decrease for the same value of recall, depending on the class of the instances added to or removed from the predicted positive set.
including a negative-class instance in the predicted positives drops precision without affecting recall, whereas including a positive-class instance can improve precision.
This dynamic causes the Precision-Recall (PR) curve to exhibit a zigzag pattern rather than being a smooth, monotonically increasing curve like the ROC curve.
The PR curve is sensitive to the skew factor, defined as the ratio of positives to the total number of instances (P / (P + N))
different PR curves are generated for different values of this skew factor.
Both precision and recall can be viewed as special cases of the Fβ measure by setting β=0 and β=∞, respectively.
A cluster is fundamentally defined as a set of objects in which each object is closer (or more similar) to every other object in the cluster than to any object not in the cluster.
This idealistic definition is satisfied only when the data contains natural clusters that are quite far from each other, and well-separated clusters do not need to be globular but can have any shape.
Sometimes a threshold is used to specify that all the objects in a cluster must be sufficiently close (or similar) to one another.
More generally, a cluster can be defined as a set of objects that share some property.
For example, objects in a center-based cluster share the property that they are all closest to the same centroid or medoid.
In this prototype-based approach, a cluster is a set of objects in which each object is closer (more similar) to the prototype that defines the cluster than to the prototype of any other cluster.
For data with continuous attributes, the prototype is often a centroid, i.e., the average (mean) of all the points in the cluster.
When a centroid is not meaningful, such as when the data has categorical attributes, the prototype is often a medoid, i.e., the most representative point of a cluster.
Such clusters tend to be globular.

If the data is represented as a graph, where the nodes are objects and the links represent connections among objects, a cluster can be defined as a connected component; i.e., a group of objects that are connected to one another, but that have no connection to objects outside the group.
An important example of graph-based clusters is a contiguity-based cluster, where two objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance of each other.
This definition is useful when clusters are irregular or intertwined, but it can have trouble when noise is present since a small bridge of points can merge two distinct clusters.
A density-based definition of a cluster describes it as a dense region of objects that is surrounded by a region of low density.
This definition is often employed when the clusters are irregular or intertwined, and when noise and outliers are present.
By contrast, a contiguity-based definition would not work well for such data because the noise would tend to form bridges between clusters.
In many applications, the notion of a cluster is not well defined, and the best definition depends on the nature of data and the desired results.
The process of finding clusters that require a very specific concept of a cluster to be successfully detected is called conceptual clustering.
However, too sophisticated a notion of a cluster would take us into the area of pattern recognition, and thus, simpler types of clusters are typically considered in standard data mining contexts.
Intra-cluster distance, also referred to as intra-cluster dissimilarity, measures the internal cohesion of a cluster by quantifying the distances between objects and the cluster's centroid.
In K-means clustering, this metric is calculated as the summation of distances between the objects and the centroid of the cluster to which they are assigned.
The centroid represents the mean value of the objects within that cluster.
The primary objective of clustering is to divide a data set into groups based on object similarity while minimizing this intra-cluster dissimilarity.
The distance between a centroid and an object is denoted as d(vk, xi), where vk is the centroid of cluster k and xi is the object.

The KMI procedure involves randomly selecting K complete data objects as centroids, iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of distances for each object from its cluster centroid, and finally filling in non-reference attributes for incomplete objects using a nearest neighbor algorithm.
The process terminates when the summation of distances falls below a user-specified threshold or when no changes occur to the centroids in the last iteration.

In hierarchical clustering, intra-cluster distances are explicitly excluded from inter-cluster distance calculations; for example, distances between points within the same cluster are not used to determine the height at which two distinct clusters are merged in a dendrogram.
Clustering generally requires a meaningful distance or similarity measure to function effectively.
Inter-cluster distance is a measure of proximity or dissimilarity between two distinct clusters, used in hierarchical clustering and evaluation metrics.
In the CURE algorithm, the distance between two clusters is defined as the minimum distance between any two representative points after those points are shrunk toward their respective centers.
This approach is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering under specific conditions and roughly the same as single-link hierarchical clustering under others.
In silhouette coefficient calculations, the inter-cluster component is represented by b(x), which is the smallest average distance from a point x to the members of any other cluster.
This contrasts with the intra-cluster component, which is the average distance from x to the other points in its own cluster.
In BIRCH, the distance between clusters can be computed using summary statistics, and the diameter (variance) of the merged cluster can also be used as a distance measure.
Inter-cluster distance uses only cross-cluster pairs, excluding distances inside the same cluster.

The height at which two clusters are merged in a dendrogram reflects the distance of the two clusters, as seen in single-link techniques where the distance between points or clusters determines the merge height.
The distinction between classification and clustering is defined by the source of the labels used to group objects.

Classification involves assigning particular objects to pre-existing groups, a process that relies on a model developed from objects with known class labels to assign labels to new, unlabeled objects.
clustering involves dividing objects into groups based on shared common characteristics, where the labels are derived solely from the data itself.
Because clustering creates a labeling of objects with class (cluster) labels without using pre-existing known labels, it is sometimes referred to as unsupervised classification.

While both processes result in objects being grouped, clustering is the study of techniques for automatically finding these classes, whereas classification is the assignment of objects to those classes.
This distinction is a core concept in understanding how data mining techniques divide data objects into groups.
A distance function d(x, y) between two points x and y is characterized by three well-known properties: positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality.
Positivity requires that d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y, and that d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y.
d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y
d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y
Symmetry requires that d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y.
d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y
The triangle inequality requires that d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z.
d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z
These properties are common to all distances, including the Euclidean distance.
A dissimilarity measure that fails to satisfy these properties can be modified to become a valid distance function.

For example, the measure d(A, B) = size(A - B) between two sets A and B, where size returns the number of elements in a set, is an integer value greater than or equal to 0 but does not satisfy the second part of the positivity property, the symmetry property, or the triangle inequality.
This measure can be modified to d(A, B) = size(A - B) + size(B - A) to make these properties hold.
In the case of A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {2, 3, 4}, A - B = {1} and B - A = ∅, so the original measure gives d(A, B) = 1, while the modified measure gives d(A, B) = 1.
The distance function is assumed to return a distance of 0 only for objects that are the same, which is a condition relevant to algorithms that rely on distance comparisons.
A similarity function s(x, y) measures the similarity between points x and y.
The typical properties of similarities are symmetry and positivity, whereas the triangle inequality (or the analogous property) typically does not hold.
s(x, y) = 1 only if x = y, with the constraint 0 ≤ s ≤ 1
a similarity value of 1 implies the points are identical, and the similarity value is bounded between 0 and 1
The evidence does not provide a formal symbolic statement for the symmetry and positivity properties, nor does it define the specific conditions under which the triangle inequality fails.
The similarity of interval or ratio attributes is typically expressed by transforming a dissimilarity into a similarity.
dissimilarity measures can be modified to satisfy certain properties, such as using d(A, B) = size(A-B) + size(B-A) to ensure symmetry
Euclidean distance is a metric distance measure used to quantify the proximity between two points in Euclidean space.
It is a specific case of the Lp norm distance family and is the most commonly used proximity measure in the literature for dense, continuous data.
The measure is defined by the formula d_E(x, y) = sqrt((x_1 - y_1)^2 + (x_2 - y_2)^2), where x and y are the coordinates of the two points.

As a distance function, it satisfies the properties of positivity (d(x, y) ≥ 0), identity of indiscernibles (d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y), symmetry (d(x, y) = d(y, x)), and the triangle inequality (d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z)).

In clustering algorithms such as K-means, Euclidean distance is used to determine the closest centroid for each data point and to compute the sum of squared errors (SSE) as an objective function for evaluating cluster quality.

It is distinct from similarity measures like cosine similarity, which compares direction or pattern rather than location, and from other distance metrics like Manhattan distance, which measures distance by moving step-by-step along the axes.

Manhattan distance is a distance measure that quantifies the separation between two points by summing the absolute differences of their coordinates, effectively measuring the distance if one moves step by step along the axes, like walking through city blocks.
d_Manhattan(x, y) = Σ_{i=1}^{m} |x_i - y_i|
x and y are the points being compared, m is the number of dimensions, and x_i and y_i are the coordinates of the points in the i-th dimension
This measure is distinct from similarity scores, such as cosine similarity, where larger values indicate greater similarity, whereas Manhattan distance is a distance metric.
The value of Manhattan distance is always non-negative and finite, satisfying the condition 0 ≤ d_Manhattan(x, y) < ∞
In the context of clustering, when the objective is to minimize the sum of distances, the appropriate centroid for a cluster using Manhattan distance is the median of the points in that cluster
Cosine similarity is a similarity score, distinct from distance measures like Manhattan and Euclidean distance, where a larger value indicates greater similarity.
It measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, x and y.
When the cosine similarity is 1, the angle between the vectors is 0 degrees, meaning they point in the same direction and are identical except for length.
When the cosine similarity is 0, the angle is 90 degrees, indicating the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms.
When the cosine similarity is -1, the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.
The calculation involves normalizing the vectors by dividing them by their lengths, which results in vectors of length 1.
This normalization means cosine similarity does not take the length of the data objects into account.
For unit-length vectors, the cosine measure is calculated by taking a simple inner product.
This approach is useful for sparse data, such as documents represented as vectors where components record word frequencies, and can reduce computation time when many similarities are calculated.
In the context of clustering, cosine similarity is used as a proximity measure in K-means style algorithms, where the objective is to maximize the similarity of objects to the cluster centroid.
It is also included in the class of Bregman divergences, which can serve as the basis for clustering algorithms with convergence properties similar to standard K-means.
The Rand Index is an external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the cluster structure against true class labels.
It is a similarity-oriented measure that operates by comparing pairs of objects.
The index is calculated using the formula: Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00).
In this formula, f00 represents the pairs of objects that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering.

The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, which distinguishes it from the Jaccard Coefficient, a sibling measure that ignores f00 and focuses only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
Consequently, the Rand Index is often higher than the Jaccard Coefficient.
The calculation counts only pairs of distinct objects; self-pairs are not included in the Rand Index computation.
The Rand Index does not require the original feature values once the cluster assignments and class labels are available.
It is computed through class similarity and cluster similarity matrices.
An adjusted version of the Rand Index exists and is based on the multivariate hypergeometric distribution, which can be used to compute a p-value.

The Jaccard coefficient is a similarity measure used to evaluate the similarity between two binary vectors, particularly in contexts involving asymmetric binary attributes such as transaction data where a 1 indicates an item was purchased and a 0 indicates it was not.
It is frequently employed as a cluster validity measure and is often symbolized by j.
The coefficient is defined by the formula Jaccard Coefficient = f11 / (f11 + f10 + f01), where f11, f10, and f01 represent specific frequency counts from a contingency table.
A key characteristic of the Jaccard coefficient is that it ignores f00, focusing only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
This distinguishes it from other measures like the Rand statistic (or Simple Matching Coefficient), which includes f00 in its calculation.
For example, given f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2 / (2 + 2 + 2) = 0.33.

The measure can be extended to more than two variables using multidimensional contingency tables, and an extended version, known as the Extended Jaccard Coefficient or Tanimoto Coefficient, is used for document data and reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient for binary attributes.
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set.
The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity.
Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity.
This scaling is frequently achieved through linear transformations that map the original range of similarity or dissimilarity values to [0, 1], preserving the relative distances between points.
In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix.
The ideal matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the corresponding pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise.

When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, the ideal cluster similarity matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere.
The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known in the clustering validation literature as Hubert's Γ statistic.
The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results.
By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships and separation between clusters.
For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks.

Additionally, in supervised or semi-supervised contexts, the cluster similarity matrix can be compared against a class similarity matrix—defined as 1 if two objects belong to the same class and 0 otherwise—to derive validity measures such as the Rand Index or Jaccard Coefficient.
In these pair-by-pair comparisons, diagonal entries (comparing an object to itself) are typically excluded, as only pairs of distinct objects are counted.
K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that directly divides data into K clusters, where K is a user-specified parameter representing the desired number of clusters.
Each cluster is represented by a centroid, which is the representative centre of the cluster.
For Euclidean K-Means, the centroid is defined as the mean of all points in the cluster; it is a mean position and does not have to be one of the original data points.
If a cluster C_i contains m_i points, the centroid c_i is calculated as the mean of the points in that cluster: c_i = (1/m_i) * Σ_{x ∈ C_i} x.
In two-dimensional space, this is expressed as c_i = (Σx/m_i, Σy/m_i).
The algorithm operates by repeatedly assigning each point to the nearest centroid and then updating each centroid as the mean of the points assigned to it.
This process of assignment and update is repeated until the assignments or centroids stop changing.
K-Means is a centroid-based algorithm, and its behavior is characterized by the use of centroid-based cohesion and separation.
The algorithm is simple and is guaranteed to converge for a number of choices of proximity function, centroid, and objective function.
However, random initialization is often used, which is simple but can result in a clustering that represents a local minimum in terms of the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).
The SSE Optimization Criterion is an objective function used in clustering that aims to minimize the total squared error (SSE).
When applied to clustering, this criterion frames the task as an optimization problem where the goal is to find a partition of points that minimizes the total SSE.
The evidence indicates that finding the global optimum for this criterion is computationally infeasible because it would require enumerating all possible ways of dividing points into clusters.
Consequently, practical clustering algorithms, such as agglomerative hierarchical clustering, use local criteria to decide which clusters to merge at each step.
This local approach avoids the difficulty of solving the hard combinatorial optimization problem associated with the global SSE minimization.

For instance, Ward’s method uses the “minimize squared error” criterion to decide which clusters to merge, although the resulting clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE.
The criterion is also relevant to K-means clustering, where it serves as the objective function.

The evidence notes that a local “minimize squared error” objective function has a connection to a global “minimize squared error” objective function, as Ward’s method is often used to initialize K-means clustering.

The distinction between global and local minima is illustrated by examples where a clustering solution can be a global minimum of the SSE for a given number of clusters, while another solution is only a local minimum.
K-Means Complexity refers to the computational resource requirements of the K-means algorithm, specifically its time and space complexity.
The space requirements for K-means are modest because the algorithm stores only the data points and centroids.
The storage required is O((m+K)n), where m is the number of points, K is the number of clusters, and n is the number of attributes.
The time requirements for K-means are also modest and are basically linear in the number of data points.
The time required is O(I×K×m×n), where I is the number of iterations required for convergence.
Consequently, K-means is linear in m, the number of points, and is considered efficient and simple provided that K, the number of clusters, is significantly less than m.
The source text indicates that the K-means algorithm has a time complexity, but the specific value is missing from the provided evidence.

Additionally, the source poses questions regarding the change in time complexity as the number of clusters increases and comparisons with fuzzy c-means, but does not provide the answers or specific formulas for these scenarios in the supplied passages.

Centroid Initialization Sensitivity refers to the susceptibility of K-means clustering algorithms to the specific choice of initial centroids, a factor that can significantly impact the resulting cluster quality and Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).

Standard K-means is particularly prone to this issue, whereas variants like bisecting K-means are less susceptible because they perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest SSE, maintaining only two centroids at each step.
To mitigate this sensitivity, specific initialization procedures are employed.

One approach involves selecting the first point at random or as the centroid of all points, then iteratively selecting the point farthest from any already-selected initial centroid to ensure well-separated centroids; this method is often applied to a sample of points to avoid selecting outliers and to reduce computational expense.

Another advanced technique, K-means++, picks centroids incrementally where each point has a probability of being selected as a new centroid proportional to the square of its distance to its closest centroid, a method guaranteed to find a solution optimal to within a factor of O log(k).

These strategies address the core limitation that random initialization may lead to suboptimal clustering or the selection of outliers, which can reduce the number of centroids available for forming clusters for the majority of points.
K-Means and its variations have a number of limitations with respect to finding different types of clusters.
K-means has difficulty detecting the 'natural' clusters, when clusters have non-spherical shapes or widely different sizes or densities.

K-means cannot find the three natural clusters because one of the clusters is much larger than the other two, and hence, the larger cluster is broken, while one of the smaller clusters is combined with a portion of the larger cluster.
K-means fails to find the three natural clusters because the two smaller clusters are much denser than the larger cluster.
K-means finds two clusters that mix portions of the two natural clusters because the shape of the natural clusters is not globular.
Traditional K-means has a number of limitations, such as sensitivity to outliers and difficulty in handling clusters of different sizes and densities, or with non-globular shapes.
K-Means needs a meaningful distance and a meaningful mean.
Raw categories do not have meaningful averages.
A local minimum means K-Means cannot improve from its current path.
A global minimum means no possible clustering with the same K has lower total SSE.
Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by producing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits.
Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points.
The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2.
This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached.

A key characteristic of this approach is that it makes local split decisions, meaning it does not jointly optimize all centroids at once; consequently, it can produce different results than standard K-Means with the same target number of clusters.

The algorithm is often used to speed up clustering by reducing the number of similarity computations, as it only calculates distances for a subset of points to two centroids at each step rather than all points to all centroids.
It is also noted for being less susceptible to initialization problems because it can perform several trial bisections and select the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).

If a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from Bisecting K-Means can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step, although Bisecting K-Means itself is a valid standalone algorithm.
A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to graphically display hierarchical clustering.
It visualizes both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which clusters were merged (agglomerative view) or split (divisive view).
In the diagram, the vertical height at which two clusters are merged reflects the distance between those two clusters.
For example, if the distance between two points is 0.11, they are joined at a height of 0.11 in the dendrogram.
Hierarchical clustering is sometimes used to generate K clusters by taking the clusters at the K-th level of the dendrogram, where the root is at level 1.
This allows for the evaluation of hierarchical clustering behavior and comparison with K-means.
If a final flat clustering is desired, the dendrogram must be cut at a specific level.
When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the exact horizontal spacing does not matter, but the vertical merge heights and nested structure are critical.
The leaf order must match the nested structure exactly, though branches can be flipped left-to-right.
The dendrogram is distinct from the linkage criteria (such as single link, complete link, or group average) used to calculate the distances that determine the merge heights.

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that produces a hierarchical clustering by starting with each point as a singleton cluster and repeatedly merging the two closest clusters until a single, all-encompassing cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached.
This approach is a collection of closely related techniques where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm used.

Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity.
d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y)

Other merging strategies include the centroid method, which merges the clusters with the closest centroids, and Ward's method, which is a greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective to merge the two clusters that result in the smallest increase in total SSE.
Agglomerative clustering is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward; in contrast, agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward.

A key limitation of agglomerative hierarchical clustering is that it can never separate objects that have been wrongly put together, meaning it will only compound errors if the initial partitioning or merging decisions are incorrect.

if the data is very large, an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique cannot be directly applied, often necessitating the use of divisive techniques or other methods like BIRCH that do not require all data to be in main memory.

Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached.
This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism.
Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available.

One specific divisive hierarchical technique is the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering.
Divisive clustering is often considered when data is very large and agglomerative techniques cannot be directly applied, though the MST algorithm only works if the data set is not too large.
Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, but it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory.
In such large-scale situations, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful.

The choice of clustering algorithm is often determined by the need to create a hierarchical clustering that extends only to the point of splitting data into a few hundred clusters rather than a complete hierarchy to individual objects.
MIN (Single Linkage) is a linkage criterion used in hierarchical clustering to define the proximity between two clusters.
The proximity of two clusters is defined as the minimum of the distance (or the maximum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters.
dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min d(x, y), where the minimum is taken over all pairs x in Ci and y in Cj.

In this formula, dsingle(Ci, Cj) represents the single-linkage distance between clusters Ci and Cj, d(x, y) is the distance between individual points x and y, and the minimization is performed over all x in Ci and y in Cj.
The single-linkage technique operates by starting with all points as singleton clusters and adding links between points one at a time, shortest links first, which combines the points into clusters.
This method is characterized by the 'nearest bridge' intuition, meaning two clusters are considered close if at least one point in one cluster is close to at least one point in the other cluster.

In terms of implementation, single linkage can use a precomputed distance matrix; the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using the minimum value.
The single-linkage technique is good at handling non-elliptical shapes, but it is sensitive to noise and outliers.
It is distinct from complete linkage, which uses the farthest cross-pair, and centroid linkage, which uses the cluster centers.

MAX (Complete Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering in which the proximity of two clusters is defined as the maximum of the distance (or the minimum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters.

In graph terminology, if one starts with all points as singleton clusters and adds links between points one at a time, shortest links first, a group of points is not considered a cluster until all the points in it are completely linked, meaning they form a clique.
This method is less susceptible to noise and outliers, but it can break large clusters and it favors globular shapes.
d_complete({A, B}, C) = max(2, 1) = 2
d_complete({A, B, C, D}, E) = max(4, 3, 2, 1) = 4
The procedure for complete linkage involves computing the original point-distance matrix once, and after a merge, updating the current matrix using the maximum value.
Complete linkage says two clusters are close only if even the farthest cross-cluster pair is not too far.
This contrasts with single linkage, which uses the nearest bridge, and centroid linkage, which uses the cluster centers.

Group Average Linkage is a graph-based agglomerative clustering technique that defines the proximity between two clusters as the average of the pairwise proximities (or average length of edges) of all pairs of points from different clusters.

This approach bases its notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters, such as the pairwise similarity of points, rather than relying solely on the closeness of the clusters measured by the minimum distance between points.

In a full agglomerative clustering run, the distance between two specified clusters is calculated as one candidate distance, which must be compared with all other current cluster-pair distances before choosing a merge.
The weighted version of group average, known as WPGMA, uses coefficients that are constants independent of cluster sizes, specifically alpha_A = 1/2, alpha_B = 1/2, beta = 0, and gamma = 0.
General unweighted approaches are preferred unless there is reason to believe that individual points should have different weights.

For clustering approaches like group average, outliers are potentially less problematic because they tend to form singleton or small clusters that do not merge with other clusters until much later in the merging process, allowing them to be removed by discarding these small clusters.
Ward's method is a greedy bottom-up hierarchical clustering technique that uses the same objective function as K-means clustering: minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE).
In this approach, each cluster is represented by its centroid, and the proximity between two clusters is defined as the increase in the total SSE that results from merging them.

The algorithm proceeds by repeatedly evaluating all possible merges of existing clusters, computing the total SSE after each candidate merge, and selecting the merge that causes the smallest increase in total SSE.
This process builds a hierarchy of clusters until all points are merged into a single cluster.
The SSE for a cluster C is defined as the sum of the squared distances of its points from the cluster centroid: SSE(C) = Σ ||x - μ_C||², where x is a point in C and μ_C is the centroid of C.
The total SSE across all clusters is the sum of the individual cluster SSEs: SSE_total = SSE(C₁) + SSE(C₂) + ... + SSE(Cₖ).
Ward's method is distinct from centroid linkage, which also uses centroids but defines cluster proximity as the distance between centroids rather than the increase in SSE.
Ward's method is mathematically similar to the group average method when the proximity between two points is taken to be the square of the distance between them.
However, Ward's method is the correct hierarchical analog of K-means, as it directly optimizes the same SSE objective.
A key limitation of Ward's method is that once a merge is made, it cannot be undone, which prevents a local optimization criterion from becoming a global one.
The clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE, and a point in one cluster can be closer to the centroid of another cluster than to its own.
Despite this, Ward's method is often used as a robust method for initializing K-means clustering.

Outliers pose the most serious problems for Ward's method because they increase SSE and distort centroids, whereas in methods like single link, complete link, and group average, outliers tend to form singleton clusters that can be discarded.

Hierarchical clustering complexity refers to the computational and storage requirements of agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms, which are defined by their use of a proximity matrix and iterative merging of clusters.

The total space complexity is O(m²), where m is the number of data points, because the algorithm must store the proximities between all pairs of points (assuming a symmetric matrix) and track the state of the clusters.

The time complexity is O(m² log m) when using a sorted list or heap to optimize the search for the two closest clusters; without such optimization, the time complexity is higher due to linear searches over the proximity matrix.
These complexity bounds severely limit the size of data sets that can be processed directly, making the algorithm impractical for large-scale applications.

The high computational cost arises because the general clustering problem is computationally infeasible to solve exactly, and the local merging strategy, while avoiding hard combinatorial optimization, still incurs significant overhead.

Scalable alternatives, such as bisecting K-means or graph sparsification techniques, are often used to address these limitations by reducing the effective number of points or partitions before applying hierarchical methods.
A core point is a data point located in the interior of a density-based cluster.
a point is a core point if there are at least MinPts points within a distance of Eps, where MinPts and Eps are user-specified parameters.
The count of points in the neighborhood includes the point itself.
core points are defined as points that strongly belong to one cluster.
A core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point.
any two core points that are close enough—within a distance Eps of one another—are put in the same cluster.
The use of core points adds considerable power and flexibility to density-based clustering approaches.

A border point is a data point that is not a core point because it does not have enough points in its neighborhood to satisfy the core point condition, but it falls within the neighborhood of at least one core point.
In the context of density-based clustering, a border point is located on the edge of a dense region.
While a core point starts and expands dense regions, a border point can be attached to a dense region but does not expand it.

This limitation exists because direct density-reachability requires the starting point to be a core point; consequently, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point.
In cluster construction, border points attach to the core component formed by mutually connected core points.

If a border point is close to core points from different clusters, a border tie occurs, requiring a convention to resolve the assignment, such as assigning the point to the first cluster that reaches it or the closest core point.
A border point is distinct from a noise point, which is neither a core point nor a border point and is not assigned to any cluster.
In the context of density-based clustering, a noise point is defined as any point that is neither a core point nor a border point.

This classification arises from a center-based approach to density, which categorizes data points into three distinct types: those in the interior of a dense region (core points), those on the edge of a dense region (border points), and those in sparsely occupied regions (noise or background points).

A noise point is specifically characterized by its location in a sparsely occupied region, meaning it does not meet the density requirements to be a core point and is not within the neighborhood of a core point to qualify as a border point.
In the DBSCAN algorithm, noise points are handled by being discarded or omitted from the clustering process.
This mechanism allows the algorithm to automatically classify low-density points as noise and remove them, thereby eliminating their negative effects on the clustering results.

atypical points or outliers can severely degrade the performance of clustering algorithms, especially prototype-based methods like K-means, or cause techniques like single link to join clusters that should not be joined.
By identifying and discarding noise points, DBSCAN maintains the integrity of the discovered clusters.
The classification of a point as noise is sensitive to the algorithm's parameters.
If the distance threshold (epsilon) is set too small, most neighborhoods become too small, causing many points to be classified as noise.
If the minimum points parameter (minPts) is set too large, real small clusters may disappear and be classified as noise.
a noise point is a point that fails to satisfy the density connectivity conditions required to be part of a cluster under the given parameter settings.
DBSCAN requires two user-specified parameters, Eps and MinPts, to define its clustering behavior.
Eps represents the maximum distance threshold for neighborhood calculations, while MinPts is the minimum number of points required within that Eps radius for a point to be classified as a core point.
The point itself is included in the count of points within the Eps-neighborhood.
For example, if MinPts is set to 3, a point must have itself and at least two other points within the Eps distance to be considered core.
These parameters are global, meaning a single Eps and MinPts value are applied to the entire dataset.
The selection of these parameters is critical because they determine the density threshold used to distinguish clusters from noise.

A common method for determining Eps involves computing the k-dist (the distance to the k-th nearest neighbor) for all points, sorting these values, and identifying a sharp increase in the plot, which indicates a suitable Eps value.
The value of k used in this process typically corresponds to the MinPts parameter.

DBSCAN's reliance on a single global density threshold can be a limitation when cluster densities vary widely, as it may fail to separate clusters of different densities or merge them incorrectly depending on the chosen Eps.
A point q is directly density-reachable from a point p if and only if two conditions are met: q must be in the ε-neighborhood of p (denoted as q ∈ Nε(p)), and p must be a core point.
This relationship is asymmetric; specifically, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point.
while a border point can be assigned to a cluster, it does not expand the cluster because the definition requires the starting point of the reachability relation to be core.
a point q is density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points from p to q such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous one.

A point q is considered density-reachable from p if there exists a chain of points starting at p and ending at q, denoted as p = p1, p2, ..., pn = q, such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the preceding point.
a point q is directly density-reachable from p if q is contained in the epsilon-neighborhood of p (q ∈ Nε(p)) and p is a core point
Density-reachability is distinct from density-connectedness, which holds when there exists some point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o
The framework assumes that the entire dataset can be evaluated using a single density standard
This approach contrasts with centroid-based methods like K-means, which may identify dense compact blobs but optimize for centroid compactness rather than density reachability
Density-connected is a relationship between two points in a density-based clustering context.
Two points, p and q, are density-connected if there exists some point o such that both p and q are density-reachable from o.
a point q is density-reachable from p if there is a chain of points from p to q such that each subsequent point in the chain is directly density-reachable from the previous one.
The relationship is symmetric: if p and q are density-connected, they belong to the same cluster.
DBSCAN identifies clusters as dense regions of objects surrounded by low-density regions.
Unlike centroid-based methods that may cut through curved dense shapes, DBSCAN can follow dense connected regions when parameters are suitable.
Density-connectedness allows DBSCAN to label points as noise instead of forcing them into a cluster, which is an advantage over K-means when density connectivity is the appropriate cluster model.
DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that locates regions of high density separated by regions of low density.
Unlike K-means, which uses a prototype-based or centroid-based notion of a cluster, DBSCAN defines clusters based on a single density threshold.
This approach allows DBSCAN to handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes and makes it relatively resistant to noise.
DBSCAN produces a partitional clustering where the number of clusters is automatically determined by the algorithm, rather than being specified as a parameter.
A key characteristic of this definition is that points in low-density regions are classified as noise and omitted; consequently, DBSCAN does not produce a complete clustering of all objects.

The algorithm operates by connecting core points that are within a distance Eps of one another into the same cluster, attaching border points that are close enough to a core point to that core point's cluster, and discarding noise points.

Because it relies on a global density threshold, DBSCAN may struggle with data where cluster characteristics vary widely, and it can be computationally expensive for high-dimensional data where density is difficult to define.
DBSCAN is a density-based clustering algorithm that is relatively resistant to noise and can handle clusters of arbitrary shapes and sizes.
Because it uses a density-based definition of a cluster, it can find many clusters that could not be found using K-means.
DBSCAN is better when the density-cluster assumption matches the data, specifically when density connectivity is the right cluster model.
It can label points as noise instead of forcing them into a cluster, unlike K-means which assigns every point to some centroid.
However, DBSCAN has trouble with high-dimensional data because density is more difficult to define for such data.
It can also be computationally expensive when the computation of nearest neighbors requires computing all pairwise proximities, as is usually the case for high-dimensional data.
DBSCAN is a special case of DENCLUE, which provides a more flexible and potentially more accurate way to compute density.
Neither DBSCAN nor K-means is universally better; K-means is better when the centroid-cluster assumption matches the data, such as when clusters are compact and centroid-like.
Internal indices are unsupervised measures of cluster validity that evaluate the goodness of a clustering structure without respect to external information.
These measures are termed internal indices because they rely exclusively on information present in the data set itself.

Unsupervised measures of cluster validity are often further divided into two classes: measures of cluster cohesion, which determine how closely related the objects in a cluster are, and measures of cluster separation, which determine how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters.

Within the broader classification of cluster validity indices, internal indices represent the category that assesses clustering quality based solely on internal data characteristics rather than external reference labels.
SSE is an unsupervised, internal cluster evaluation measure that quantifies the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external information.
It functions as a centroid-quality measure, assessing how tightly data points sit around their assigned centroids; a smaller SSE indicates that points are closer to their centroids.
In the context of K-means clustering, SSE serves as the objective function to be minimized, and for a fixed number of clusters (K), a lower SSE represents a better clustering solution.
The formal definition of SSE is the sum of the squared distances between each point and its assigned cluster centroid.
SSE = ∑(i=1 to K) ∑(x ∈ Ci) (ci - x)², where K is the number of clusters, Ci is the set of points in cluster i, ci is the centroid of cluster i, and x is a data point.
SSE = ∑(i=1 to K) ∑(x ∈ Ci) dist(ci, x)².
The total SSE of a clustering is the sum of the SSE contributed by each individual cluster.
SSE is sensitive to the number of clusters used.
Increasing the number of clusters (K) almost always reduces the SSE.
In the extreme case where K equals the total number of points (n), every point becomes its own cluster, resulting in an SSE of 0, which is generally considered a useless clustering.
Because of this property, SSE can be used to determine the number of clusters by observing where the measure stops decreasing significantly as K increases.
While K-means typically converges to a local minimum of SSE, various postprocessing techniques can be used to 'fix up' the resulting clusters to achieve a lower SSE without increasing K.
These techniques include alternating phases of splitting and merging clusters.

Splitting strategies often involve dividing the cluster with the largest SSE or the largest standard deviation for a specific attribute, and introducing a new centroid (often the point farthest from any existing center).
Merging strategies combine clusters to reduce the total number while attempting to minimize the overall SSE.
Additionally, per-cluster SSE is useful as a diagnostic tool to identify which specific clusters are loose or spread out.
Cohesion is an internal measure of cluster validity that quantifies how closely related the objects within a single cluster are, often described as the compactness or tightness of the group.
It is used to evaluate the goodness of a clustering structure without relying on external labels, using only information present in the dataset.
Cohesion is distinct from separation, which measures how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters.
For prototype-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the proximity between each object in the cluster and the cluster's prototype (centroid).

cohesion(C_i) = ∑_{x∈C_i} proximity(x, c_i), where C_i is the cluster, c_i is the prototype or centroid of the cluster, and proximity is a function that can represent either similarity or dissimilarity.
When proximity is defined as squared Euclidean distance, this measure is equivalent to the cluster Sum of Squared Errors (SSE).
For graph-based clusters, cohesion is defined as the sum of the pairwise proximities between all objects in the cluster, expressed as cohesion(C_i) = ∑_{x∈C_i} ∑_{y∈C_i} proximity(x, y).
The interpretation of the cohesion value depends on the type of proximity function used.
If the proximity function is a similarity measure, higher values indicate better cohesion.
If the proximity function is a dissimilarity measure, lower values indicate better cohesion.
In the context of K-means clustering, which is a centroid-based algorithm, centroid-based cohesion is the appropriate measure.

For non-Euclidean data, such as document data represented as a document-term matrix, cohesion can be defined using cosine similarity, where the objective is to maximize the similarity of documents to the cluster centroid.
The total cohesion across all clusters is the sum of the cohesion of each individual cluster.
Cohesion is often related to separation.
For some validity measures, the sum of total SSE (cohesion) and total SSB (separation) is a constant, meaning that minimizing cohesion is equivalent to maximizing separation.

Cohesion can also be used to evaluate individual objects within a cluster; objects that contribute more to the overall cohesion are typically near the interior of the cluster, while those contributing less are near the edge.
This information can guide clustering improvements, such as splitting a cluster with low cohesion into subclusters or merging clusters that are cohesive but not well separated.
Separation is an internal cluster validity measure that quantifies how distinct or well-separated a cluster is from other clusters.
It is used to evaluate clustering quality by assessing the distance or dissimilarity between clusters, often in conjunction with cohesion measures.

For prototype-based clusters, such as those produced by K-Means, separation is defined as the proximity (distance or dissimilarity) between the cluster's prototype (centroid or medoid) and either another cluster's prototype or an overall prototype.
Specifically, the separation between two clusters Ci and Cj is given by separation(Ci, Cj) = proximity(ci, cj), where ci and cj are the prototypes of the respective clusters.
Alternatively, the separation of a single cluster Ci from the overall dataset is given by separation(Ci) = proximity(ci, c), where c is the overall prototype.

In graph-based or object-level definitions, separation is calculated as the sum of pairwise proximities between all objects in one cluster and all objects in another cluster: separation(Ci, Cj) = ∑_{x∈Ci} ∑_{y∈Cj} proximity(x, y).

Another formulation, often used in normalized contexts, defines separation(Y) as the average normalized distance from a cluster's centroid to the centroids of all other clusters: separation(Y) = (1 / (|ζ| - 1)) ∑_{Y'∈ζ, Y'≠Y} d_N(center(Y), center(Y')).

The choice of proximity function (similarity or dissimilarity) affects interpretation: for similarity, lower separation values indicate better separation; for dissimilarity, higher values indicate better separation.
Separation is distinct from cohesion, which measures internal cluster compactness, and from external indices like Rand Index or Purity, which require ground truth labels.
The silhouette coefficient is an internal cluster evaluation measure that does not use class labels.
It evaluates whether a point is closer to its own cluster than to the nearest competing cluster by combining both cohesion (compactness) and separation.
For a point x in cluster X, the coefficient is computed using two components.
First, a(x) is the average distance from x to the other points in its own cluster, defined as a(x) = (sum of d(x, u) for u in X excluding x) / (|X| - 1).
Second, for another cluster Y not equal to X, the average distance from x to the members of Y is defined as bb(x, Y) = (sum of d(x, u) for u in Y) / |Y|.
The value b(x) is the smallest average distance to another cluster, defined as b(x) = min over Y in the set of clusters excluding X of bb(x, Y).
The silhouette coefficient for point x is given by the formula: silhouette(x) = (b(x) - a(x)) / max(a(x), b(x)).
When a(x) < b(x), the denominator is b(x), and the expression can be written as (b(x) - a(x)) / b(x) = 1 - a(x)/b(x).
The value of the silhouette coefficient can vary between -1 and 1.
We want the silhouette coefficient to be positive, and for a(x) to be as close to 0 as possible, since the coefficient assumes its maximum value of 1 when a(x) = 0.
The average silhouette coefficient of a cluster is computed by taking the average of the silhouette coefficients of points belonging to the cluster.
An overall measure of the goodness of a clustering can be obtained by computing the average silhouette coefficient of all points.

When used with a partitional clustering algorithm such as K-means, the silhouette coefficient tends to decrease until the 'natural' set of clusters is found and start increasing once clusters are being split 'too finely' since separation will suffer and cohesion will not improve much.
Thus, these measures can provide a way to determine the number of clusters.

However, if the definition of a cluster used by the clustering algorithm differs from that of the cluster evaluation measure, then the set of clusters identified as optimal by the algorithm and validation measure can differ.

In addition, if there actually are subclusters that are not separated very well from one another, then methods that incorporate both cohesion and separation may provide only a coarse view of the cluster structure of the data.
The silhouette index did well on handling issues such as noise and differing sizes and density, but did not do well on handling arbitrary shapes.
Entropy is a supervised external index used in cluster evaluation to measure how well the clustering structure discovered by an algorithm matches externally supplied class labels.
It is classified as an external index because it relies on information not present in the data set itself, specifically the ground-truth class labels.

In the context of statistical testing for clustering significance, entropy serves as a test statistic to evaluate whether the observed cluster labels are significantly different from a random partitioning of the data.
Entropy = −∑i=0c−1pi(t) log2pi(t), where the summation runs over classes and the terms involve the probability of class membership.
Entropy(D) = −p+ log2(p+) −p−log2(p−), which is typically associated with decision tree node impurity rather than the multi-class cluster evaluation context defined for this unit.
Entropy is frequently cited alongside the Gini index as a popular measure of impurity.
Entropy is monotonically increasing on the range [0, 0.5] and monotonically decreasing on the range [0.5, 1], a property shared with the Gini index.

This unit is distinct from internal indices like SSE or the silhouette coefficient, which do not use external class labels, and from other external indices like Purity or F-Measure, which use different mathematical formulations to assess the match between cluster and class labels.
Purity is an external clustering validity index that measures the extent to which a cluster contains objects of a single class.

It is classified as an external index because it compares the discovered cluster labels against known class labels, distinguishing it from internal indices that are computed for unlabeled data without reference to external ground truth.
The purity of a specific cluster i is defined as the maximum fraction of that cluster consisting of objects from any single class j, expressed by the formula purity(i) = max_j p_ij.
purity(i) = max_j p_ij
The overall purity of a clustering is calculated as the weighted average of the purity of each cluster, expressed by the formula purity = ∑_{i=1}^{K} m_i purity(i).
purity = ∑_{i=1}^{K} m_i purity(i)

p_ij represents the fraction of cluster i that consists of objects of class j, calculated as m_ij / m_i, where m_ij is the number of objects in cluster i belonging to class j and m_i is the total number of objects in cluster i.
The term m_i in the overall purity formula serves as the weight for each cluster's purity, ensuring that larger clusters contribute proportionally more to the final score.

Purity is used in statistical testing procedures to measure the significance of a discovered clustering, where it can serve as a test statistic to evaluate whether the observed clustering structure is significant compared to a null hypothesis of random partitioning.

The Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient are external validation measures used to evaluate clustering by comparing the discovered cluster structure against an external structure, usually known class labels.
They are classified as similarity-oriented measures because they operate by comparing pairs of objects rather than using classification-oriented metrics like purity or F-measure.
The key distinction between the two lies in how they handle pairs that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering (denoted as f00).
The Rand Index includes these f00 pairs in its calculation, whereas the Jaccard Coefficient ignores f00 and focuses exclusively on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures.
the Rand statistic is computed as (2+4)/10 = 0.6, and the Jaccard coefficient is computed as 2/(2+2+2) = 0.33
The general methodology for computing these indices involves constructing class similarity and cluster similarity matrices.

a statistical significance assessment can be performed by generating M randomized sets of labels, computing the external index for each randomization, and defining the p-value as the fraction of randomizations where the index value exceeds the value obtained for the original set of labels.
Precision is a metric used in cluster evaluation to measure the fraction of a cluster that consists of objects of a specified class.
The precision of cluster i with respect to class j is denoted by precision(i,j) = pij.
In this notation, i represents the cluster index, j represents the class index, and pij is the value of the precision metric for that specific cluster-class pair.
The provided evidence does not define the mathematical formula for calculating pij, nor does it describe the procedure for computing it from cluster and class data.
It is distinct from internal indices such as Cohesion and Separation, which evaluate cluster quality without reference to external class labels.
Recall is an external index used in cluster evaluation to measure the extent to which a cluster contains all objects of a specified class.
It is a classification-oriented measure that assesses how well the discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels.
The recall of cluster i with respect to class j is defined by the formula recall(i,j) = m_ij / m_j, where m_j represents the number of objects in class j.

This metric is one of several external indices, including purity, precision, F-measure, and similarity-oriented measures like the Rand Index and Jaccard Coefficient, used to evaluate clustering performance against ground truth data.
The F-measure is an external index used in cluster evaluation to assess the extent to which a discovered clustering structure matches an external structure, typically known class labels.
It is a classification-oriented measure that combines both precision and recall.
The F-measure of a cluster i with respect to a class j measures the extent to which the cluster contains only objects of that particular class (precision) and all objects of that class (recall).
F(i,j) = (2 × precision(i,j) × recall(i,j)) / (precision(i,j) + recall(i,j))
In this expression, precision(i,j) and recall(i,j) are the precision and recall values for cluster i with respect to class j.
The F-measure is one of several external indices, including purity, precision, recall, Rand Index, and Jaccard Coefficient, used to evaluate clustering performance against external ground truth.
Data integration is the process of merging data elements from different sources into a single data set.
This task is required when there are several or heterogeneous sources of data, as gathering all data elements together is not an easy task.

Different attribute names or table schemes from various sources produce uneven examples that need to be consolidated, and attribute values may represent the same concept with different names, creating inconsistencies in the instances obtained.
An essential part of the integration process is to build a data map that establishes how each instance should be arranged in a common structure to present a real-world example.
When data is obtained from relational databases, it is usually flattened and gathered together into one single record.
Some database frameworks enable the user to provide a map to directly traverse the database through in-database access utilities.
While using in-database mining tools has the advantage of not having to extract and create an external file for the data, it is not the best option for its treatment with preprocessing techniques.
In this case, extracting the data is usually the best option.
Preprocessing takes time, and when the data is kept in the database, preprocessing has to be applied repeatedly.
If the data is extracted to an external file, then processing and modeling it can be faster if the data is already preprocessed and completely fits in memory.
If the integration process is not properly performed, redundancies and inconsistencies will soon appear, resulting in a decrease of the accuracy and speed of the subsequent data mining processes.

Matching the schema from different sources presents a notorious problem that usually does not come alone: inconsistent and duplicated tuples as well as redundant and correlated attributes are problems that the data set creation process will probably show sooner or later.
Automatic approaches used to integrate the data can be found in the literature, from techniques that match and find the schemas of the data to automatic procedures that reconcile different schemas.
After the data is correctly integrated into a data set, it does not mean that the data is free from errors.
The integration may result in an inordinate proportion of the data being dirty.
Broadly, dirty data include missing data, wrong data and non-standard representation of the same data.
If a high proportion of the data is dirty, applying a data mining process will surely result in an unreliable model.
Dirty data has varying degrees of impact depending on the data mining algorithm, but it is difficult to quantify such an impact.
An attribute is redundant when it can be derived from another attribute or set of them, or when it is strongly correlated with another attribute in the data.

Redundancy is a problem that should be avoided as much as possible because it usually causes an increment in the data set size, meaning that the modeling time of data mining algorithms is incremented as well, and may also induce overfitting in the obtained model.
Inconsistencies in dimension or attribute names can cause redundancies as well.

When examples come from different sources and have to be merged in a single data set, if some attributes are calculated from the others, the data sets will present a large size but the information contained will not scale accordingly, making detecting and eliminating redundant attributes needed.
Redundancies in attributes can be detected using correlation analysis, which measures how strong the implication of one attribute to the other is.
When the data is nominal and the set of values is finite, the chi-squared test is commonly applied.
In numeric attributes, the use of the correlation coefficient and the covariance is typical.

For two nominal attributes A and B containing c and r distinct values each, a contingency table is created with the joint events (Ai, Bj) in which attribute A takes the value ai and attribute B takes the value bj.

The chi-squared value is computed as the sum over i from 1 to c and j from 1 to r of (oij - eij)^2 / eij, where oij is the observed frequency of the joint event (Ai, Bj) and eij is the expected frequency of (Ai, Bj) computed as count(A = ai) × count(B = bj) / m.

Here, m is the number of instances in the data set, count(A = ai) is the number of instances with the value ai for attribute A, and count(B = bj) is the number of instances having the value bj for attribute B.
The chi-squared test checks the hypothesis that A and B are independent, with (r-1) × (c-1) degrees of freedom.
The chi-squared statistic is compared against a chi-squared table using the suitable degrees of freedom or available software.

If the significance level of the table is below the established one, or the statistic value computed is above the needed one in the table, the null hypothesis is rejected and A and B are statistically correlated.

For two numerical attributes, the correlation coefficient rA,B is computed as the sum over i from 1 to m of (ai - A_bar)(bi - B_bar) / (m σA σB), which is equivalent to (sum over i from 1 to m of (ai bi) - m A_bar B_bar) / (m σA σB).

Here, m is the number of instances, ai and bi are the values of attributes A and B in the instances, A_bar and B_bar are the mean values of A and B respectively, and σA and σB are the standard deviations of A and B.
Checking whether numerical attributes are highly correlated is useful to determine if they are redundant.
Different classifiers handle redundant attributes in different ways.

Decision trees can handle the presence of redundant attributes because redundant attributes show similar gains in purity if they are selected for splitting, so only one of them will be selected as an attribute test condition.

Logistic regression can handle redundant attributes that are duplicates of each other by learning equal weights for every redundant attribute without degrading classification performance, although a large number of irrelevant or redundant attributes in high-dimensional settings can make it susceptible to model overfitting.

Linear SVM can handle redundant attributes by learning similar weights for the duplicate attributes, and its ability to regularize its learning makes it more robust to the presence of a large number of irrelevant and redundant attributes than other classifiers.

Rule-based classifiers can easily handle the presence of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with one other because once an attribute has been used as a conjunct in a rule antecedent, the remaining redundant attributes would show little to no information gain and would thus be ignored.

Bayesian networks can easily handle the presence of correlated or redundant attributes because they do not use the naive Bayes assumption about conditional independence, but instead are able to express richer forms of conditional independence.

Artificial neural networks can handle redundant attributes by receiving similar weights for them without degrading the quality of the classifier, although if the number of irrelevant or redundant attributes is large, the learning of the ANN model may suffer from overfitting.

The presence of a large number of redundant attributes that are highly correlated with each other can bias proximity measures toward such attributes, resulting in improper estimates of distance and adversely affecting the performance of nearest neighbor classifiers.
Duplicate tuples are repeated instances of data records that appear in a dataset, often arising from the use of denormalized tables or errors in the data entry process.
These duplicates are a significant concern in data preprocessing because they waste storage space and computing time for data mining algorithms and can serve as a source of inconsistency.

A particularly difficult case occurs when entry errors cause slight differences in attribute values, such as identifier values, resulting in instances that are substantively identical but are treated as distinct; these are harder to detect than simple exact matches.

Duplicate tuples frequently emerge during the data integration process, where matching schemas from different sources can introduce redundancies and inconsistencies that degrade the accuracy and speed of subsequent data mining tasks.
While the source material identifies the detection of tuple duplication as a specific preprocessing step, it does not provide a formal algorithm or procedure for resolving these duplicates.
Inconsistent values are data quality issues where recorded attribute values differ from the true values or violate established constraints.
This can occur when information is sourced from different systems with varying measurement standards, leading to instances that are actually the same but not identified as such.
A specific form of inconsistency arises when attribute values fall outside the established range, a condition usually indicated in the associated metadata for the data set.
A common example is an address field where the specified zip code area is not contained within the listed city, which may result from transposed digits or misread handwritten forms.
In the context of duplicate detection, inconsistent values must be resolved when two objects represent a single entity but have differing attribute values.
It is important to detect and, if possible, correct such problems to ensure data integrity.
Data cleaning is the first step in data preprocessing, specifically defined as the detection and correction of data inaccuracies.
It is a necessary phase that occurs after data has become computer-readable and constitutes a unique source, but before any data mining (DM) technique is applied.
The primary goal of data cleaning is to filter or repair dirty data to ensure that the knowledge extracted by DM algorithms is accurate and that the algorithms can effectively handle the data.
Without this step, the presence of dirty data can lead to less reliable models or prevent algorithms from functioning properly.
Dirty data typically manifests in two main forms: missing data and wrong (noisy) data.
The sources of these errors include data entry errors, data update errors, data transmission errors, and bugs in the data processing system.
It is important to distinguish data cleaning from other preprocessing steps; for instance, having a uniform data set without measurable inconsistencies does not automatically mean the data is clean.

Furthermore, data cleaning is distinct from data normalization and transformation, which are used to adapt the data set to the specific needs of the DM algorithm (such as handling nominal attributes or subtle transformations) rather than correcting inaccuracies.

The impact of dirty data varies by algorithm; for example, decision trees (especially those of higher order), artificial neural networks (ANNs), and distance-based algorithms like KNN are known to be susceptible to noise.
Therefore, data cleaning is a foundational technique required to improve the accuracy and efficiency of subsequent data mining processes.
Normalization and transformation are data preprocessing techniques used to adapt a data set to the needs of a subsequent data mining algorithm.
A variable transformation is a transformation applied to all the values of a variable, meaning that for each object, the transformation is applied to the value of the variable for that object.
if only the magnitude of a variable is important, the values can be transformed by taking the absolute value.
'normalization' usually refers to a particular case of min-max normalization in which the final interval is [0, 1], meaning the new minimum is 0 and the new maximum is 1.
The interval [-1, 1] is also typical when normalizing data.
v' = new-min_A + R * ((v - min_A) / (max_A - min_A)), where max_A and min_A are the original maximum and minimum attribute values respectively.

Rescaling all data to the same range of values avoids attributes with a large max_A - min_A difference dominating over others in distance calculations, which would otherwise mislead the learning process by giving more importance to those attributes.
Normalization is also known for speeding up the learning process in artificial neural networks (ANNs), helping weights to converge faster.

In some cases, transformation or normalization of the data is needed to obtain a proper similarity measure, such as when time series have trends or periodic patterns that significantly impact similarity.

A specific transformation useful for obtaining a new variable that is very likely to behave like a normally distributed one involves using the rank of the observation and the cumulative normal function.
However, this transformation cannot be applied separately to the training and test partitions; it is only recommended when the test and training data is the same.
A missing value is a data quality issue where an attribute value or an entire data object is absent from a dataset.
This can occur because information was not collected or because certain attributes are not applicable to all objects.
Missing values are distinct from other data quality issues such as spurious or duplicate objects, and inconsistencies where data is present but logically incorrect.
Handling missing values is a critical step in data analysis because even partially specified data objects contain information, and ignoring them can make reliable analysis difficult or impossible.
The approach to handling missing values depends on the specific machine learning algorithm being used.

Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values by ignoring them during training and using only non-missing values for testing, though this can be inaccurate if the frequency of missing values depends on the class label.
Bayesian networks handle missing values by treating them as unobserved nodes and marginalizing out their effect.
logistic regression and artificial neural networks (ANN) cannot handle missing values and typically require instances with missing values to be discarded.

Decision tree classifiers offer several specific methods for handling missing values in test instances: the probabilistic split method (used by C4.5) distributes the instance to every child node based on probability; the surrogate split method (used by CART) assigns the instance to a child node based on a surrogate attribute; and the separate class method (used by CHAID) treats the missing value as a distinct categorical value.
General strategies for dealing with missing values include deletion and imputation.
Deletion involves eliminating objects or attributes with missing values, which is expedient if only a few objects are affected but risky if many are missing or if the attributes are critical.
Imputation involves estimating missing values, such as by interpolating in time series, using nearest neighbors, or using the mean (for continuous attributes) or mode (for categorical attributes).
There is no universal imputation method that performs best for all classifiers.
A missingness mechanism describes the underlying process that determines which values in a dataset are missing.

Categorizing these mechanisms is a critical step in data preprocessing because the assumptions made about the missingness mechanism and the pattern of missing values directly affect which treatment methods can be correctly applied.
The evidence specifically defines the Missing at Random (MAR) mechanism.
In the MAR case, the probability that an observation is missing may depend on the observed part of the data (Xobs) but not on the missing part (Xmis).

Formally, if X is partitioned into Xobs and Xmis, the MAR assumption implies that the distribution of the missingness indicator B, given Xobs and Xmis, is identical to the distribution of B given only Xobs.
